facts.fact: Rabbits eat grass, leaves, and other plants. Their front teeth never stop growing, so they chew tough plants to wear the teeth down.
facts.hook: a pet rabbit that only wants cake, and its teeth keep getting longer

facts.fact: A frog starts life as a tadpole that lives in water and breathes with gills like a fish. Later it grows legs and can hop onto land.
facts.hook: a tadpole who wants to join the frogs on land before it has legs

facts.fact: A snail's shell is part of its body, so a snail can never leave its shell or move into a different one.
facts.hook: a child who tries to give a snail a bigger, fancier shell

facts.fact: Bees make honey from nectar, the sweet juice they drink from flowers and carry back to their hive.
facts.hook: a bear who thinks honey comes from the store, not from flowers

facts.fact: Owls sleep during the day and hunt at night. Their feathers are so soft that they can fly almost without a sound.
facts.hook: a child who invites an owl to a picnic at noon

facts.fact: A duck spreads oil from its own body over its feathers, so water rolls off and the duck stays dry while it swims.
facts.hook: a soaking-wet child who wonders why the duck is dry

facts.fact: An elephant sucks water up into its trunk, then squirts the water into its mouth to drink. It does not drink through the trunk like a straw.
facts.hook: a child who tries to drink through a hose like an elephant

facts.fact: A newborn kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean. It crawls into its mother's pouch and grows there for months.
facts.hook: a child at the zoo looking for the big baby kangaroo

facts.fact: Spiders have eight legs, but insects like ants, bees, and beetles have six. So a spider is not an insect.
facts.hook: a child who counts legs to find out what kind of bug it is

facts.fact: Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. They use their wings like flippers to zoom through the water.
facts.hook: a child who tries to teach a penguin to fly

facts.fact: Many birds fly to warmer places when winter is coming and fly back in the spring.
facts.hook: a child who thinks the birds are lost and wants to bring them home

facts.fact: A seed needs water and warmth to sprout. The root grows down first, then the green shoot grows up toward the light.
facts.hook: a child who plants a seed upside down and worries it will grow the wrong way

facts.fact: Plants make their own food from sunlight. A plant kept in a dark closet turns pale and floppy.
facts.hook: a child who hides a plant in the closet to keep it safe

facts.fact: A cloud is made of tiny drops of water floating in the air. When the drops join up and get too heavy, they fall as rain.
facts.hook: a child who tries to catch a cloud in a jar

facts.fact: To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and the rain in front of you. Sunlight goes through the raindrops and splits into colors.
facts.hook: a child who runs toward the sun looking for the rainbow

facts.fact: Snow is frozen water. A snowball brought into a warm house melts into a puddle.
facts.hook: a child who saves a snowball in a drawer for summer

facts.fact: The sun looks small because it is very far away. It is really much, much bigger than the whole Earth.
facts.hook: a child who is sure the sun is the size of a ball

facts.fact: The moon does not make its own light. It looks bright because sunlight bounces off it.
facts.hook: a child who tries to find the moon's light switch

facts.fact: Some trees drop all their leaves in the fall and grow new ones in the spring. Pine trees keep their needles all year.
facts.hook: a child who thinks the bare tree in the yard has died

facts.fact: Lightning and thunder happen at the same time, but you see the flash before you hear the boom, because light travels faster than sound.
facts.hook: a child who counts between the flash and the boom

facts.fact: Each fluffy bit of a dandelion puff is a seed with a tiny parachute. The wind can carry the seed far away to grow somewhere new.
facts.hook: a child who blows a dandelion and worries where the seeds went

facts.fact: Wind is air that is moving. You cannot see the wind, but you can see what it pushes, like leaves, flags, and kites.
facts.hook: a child who tries to catch the wind in a bag

facts.fact: A puddle disappears on a warm day because the water slowly turns into a gas called water vapor and floats up into the air.
facts.hook: a child who guards a puddle so nobody can take it

facts.fact: Every morning the sun comes up on the east side of the sky, and every evening it goes down on the west side.
facts.hook: a child who waits for the sunset at the wrong window

facts.fact: Fog is a cloud that sits on the ground. Walking through fog means walking through a cloud.
facts.hook: a child who wants to touch a cloud and finally can on a foggy morning

facts.fact: A tree grows one new ring inside its trunk each year. You can count the rings on a cut stump to find out how old the tree was.
facts.hook: a child who counts stump rings to see if the tree was older than grandma

facts.fact: Your heart is a pump about the size of your fist. It beats faster when you run so it can send more blood to your legs.
facts.hook: a child who feels their heart thumping after a race and worries

facts.fact: Hair and fingernails keep growing all the time. Cutting them does not hurt because the parts you cut are not alive.
facts.hook: a child who is scared a haircut will hurt

facts.fact: Your nose does a lot of your tasting. When your nose is stuffed up from a cold, food tastes bland because you cannot smell it.
facts.hook: a child with a cold who thinks the soup is broken

facts.fact: Cutting an onion lets out a gas that stings your eyes, so your eyes make tears to wash it away, even if you are not sad.
facts.hook: a child who thinks dad is crying because he is sad

facts.fact: You blink about fifteen times every minute to keep your eyes wet, and you usually do not notice.
facts.hook: a staring contest where nobody can win

facts.fact: Spinning around makes you dizzy because liquid inside your ears keeps swirling for a little while after you stop.
facts.hook: a child who spins in circles and then cannot walk straight

facts.fact: Children have twenty first teeth. Starting around age six, the first teeth fall out one by one and bigger teeth grow in.
facts.hook: a four-year-old who wants a tooth to fall out right now

facts.fact: You are a tiny bit taller in the morning than at night. The soft pads between the bones in your back get squished during the day.
facts.hook: a child who measures against the wall at bedtime and again at breakfast

facts.fact: A sneeze blasts air out of your nose very fast to blow out dust or anything that tickles inside.
facts.hook: a child who sniffs pepper to see what happens

facts.fact: Your skin has tiny holes that let out sweat. As the sweat dries, it cools you down.
facts.hook: a child who thinks sweating means something is wrong

facts.fact: A scab is dried blood that makes a lid over a cut. Under the lid, new skin grows.
facts.hook: a child who wants to peel off a scab to see what is under it

facts.fact: Sound is air wiggling. The wiggles reach a thin skin inside your ear, called the eardrum, and make it shake, and that is how you hear.
facts.hook: a child who feels a drum shake and wonders if ears do the same

facts.fact: Your tummy growls when it is empty. It squeezes and moves air around inside, and the air makes the noise.
facts.hook: a child whose tummy growls during quiet time

facts.fact: The black dot in the middle of your eye is a hole called the pupil. It gets bigger in the dark to let in more light and smaller in bright light.
facts.hook: two children checking each other's eyes with a flashlight

facts.fact: The tiny lines on your fingertips are your fingerprints. No two people have the same fingerprints, not even twins.
facts.hook: a mystery about who touched the frosting

facts.fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
facts.hook: a child who counts the cookies from both ends to check

facts.fact: A triangle has three straight sides and three corners. A square has four sides that are all the same length and four corners.
facts.hook: a child sorting crackers into triangles and squares

facts.fact: A circle has no corners, so a round wheel rolls smoothly. A block with corners bumps along and stops.
facts.hook: a wagon with square wheels that will not roll

facts.fact: If you share six cookies fairly between two friends, each friend gets three cookies.
facts.hook: two friends who argue until they count out the cookies

facts.fact: Zero means none at all. If you have zero apples, your basket is empty.
facts.hook: a child looking everywhere for the zero apples

facts.fact: A tall thin glass and a short wide glass can hold the same amount of juice, even though the tall one looks like more.
facts.hook: two siblings who each want the glass with more juice

facts.fact: The same buttons can be sorted more than one way, such as by color or by size. Both ways are right.
facts.hook: two children who sort the same buttons differently and both think they won

facts.fact: A pattern repeats the same way over and over, like red, blue, red, blue. Once you know the pattern, you can say what comes next.
facts.hook: a child stringing beads who runs out of blue ones

facts.fact: Half means two pieces that are exactly the same size. If one piece is bigger, it is not half.
facts.hook: a child who cuts a cookie in half but not fairly

facts.fact: To see which of two sticks is longer, line up one end of each stick. A stick that starts farther ahead can look longer when it is not.
facts.hook: a child who thinks their stick is longer until they line them up

facts.fact: You can measure how long something is by counting how many same-sized things fit along it, like blocks or shoes.
facts.hook: a child measuring the table in shoes

facts.fact: A cube has six flat square faces. A die is a cube, with a different number of dots on each face.
facts.hook: a child who tries to count all the sides of a die

facts.fact: Bigger does not always mean heavier. A big balloon weighs less than a small rock.
facts.hook: a child who thinks the biggest present must be the heaviest

facts.fact: There is no biggest number. Whatever number you say, you can always add one more.
facts.hook: a child who claims to know the biggest number

facts.fact: A zipper has two rows of tiny teeth. The slider locks the teeth together as you pull it up, and if one tooth is bent, the zipper gets stuck.
facts.hook: a child stuck in a coat with a broken zipper

facts.fact: A magnet sticks to things made of iron or steel, like a paper clip or a fridge door. It does not stick to wood, plastic, or glass.
facts.hook: a child who tries to hang a drawing on a wooden door with a magnet

facts.fact: A fridge keeps food cold by pulling heat out of the inside and pushing it out the back. That is why the back of a fridge feels warm.
facts.hook: a child who feels the warm fridge and thinks it is broken

facts.fact: A seesaw is a lever. A small person sitting far from the middle can lift a big person sitting close to the middle.
facts.hook: a small child who lifts dad on the seesaw

facts.fact: Water alone slides off grease. Soap grabs onto grease and lets the water carry it away, so greasy hands need soap.
facts.hook: a child who washes with water only and still has sticky hands

facts.fact: A wagon moves easily because its wheels turn on a rod called an axle. Dragging the same load without wheels is much harder.
facts.hook: a child moving a pile of rocks with and without a wagon

facts.fact: Glass is made from sand. The sand is heated until it melts into a gooey liquid, shaped, and then cooled until it is hard.
facts.hook: a child at the beach who wonders if sand could become a window

facts.fact: Paper is made from trees. The wood is chopped into tiny bits, mixed with water into mush, pressed flat, and dried.
facts.hook: a child who thanks a tree for the drawing paper

facts.fact: Electricity only flows when the path is complete. A light switch opens a gap in the wire to turn the light off and closes it to turn the light on.
facts.hook: a child with a flashlight that will not work because a wire is loose

facts.fact: In a glass thermometer, the liquid inside takes up more room when it warms up, so it climbs higher in the tube.
facts.hook: a child who warms a thermometer in their hands to make it climb

facts.fact: Bread dough rises because yeast, a tiny living thing, eats sugar in the dough and makes bubbles of gas.
facts.hook: a child who watches dough grow and thinks it is alive

facts.fact: A key opens a lock because its bumps push tiny pins inside to exactly the right heights. A different key pushes them to the wrong heights.
facts.hook: a child who tries every key on the ring

facts.fact: Wool comes from sheep. The sheep get a haircut, and the wool is washed, spun into yarn, and knitted into sweaters.
facts.hook: a child who worries a freshly shorn sheep will be cold

facts.fact: When you push a toilet handle, water rushes from the tank into the bowl. The rushing water pulls everything down the pipe.
facts.hook: a child who wonders where the water goes

facts.fact: Water cannot soak into plastic, so it rolls off a raincoat. Cotton soaks water up, so a cotton sweater gets heavy and wet.
facts.hook: a child who picks a sweater instead of a raincoat

facts.fact: A fire truck's hose connects to a hydrant on the street. The hydrant is connected to big water pipes under the ground.
facts.hook: a child who wonders how the fire truck carries enough water

facts.fact: A letter dropped in a mailbox is picked up by a mail carrier, sorted at a big building, and then delivered to the address written on it.
facts.hook: a child who mails a letter to grandma without writing the address

facts.fact: Farmers grow wheat, which is ground into flour at a mill. A baker mixes the flour with water and yeast to make bread.
facts.hook: a child who thinks bread grows on trees

facts.fact: A dentist uses a tiny mirror on a stick to see the backs of your teeth, where you cannot see them yourself.
facts.hook: a child who is sure the back teeth are already clean

facts.fact: At a store, you trade money for things. The store uses that money to buy more things to sell and to pay the people who work there.
facts.hook: a child who thinks the store gives things away

facts.fact: A stop sign has eight sides. No other road sign has that shape, so drivers know it is a stop sign even from behind.
facts.hook: a child who counts the sides of every sign on the walk to school

facts.fact: Tap water comes from a river, lake, or well. It is cleaned at a water plant before it travels through pipes to your house.
facts.hook: a child who thinks the tap makes the water

facts.fact: A doctor listens to your heart and breathing with a stethoscope. The sound travels up the tubes to the doctor's ears.
facts.hook: a child who tries the stethoscope on a teddy bear

facts.fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
facts.hook: a child who wants to keep the library book forever

facts.fact: Bakers start work very early, often before the sun comes up, so the bread is ready when the shop opens.
facts.hook: a child who wakes up early to see the bread being made

facts.fact: A lighthouse shines a bright light at night so ships know where the rocky shore is and can steer away from it.
facts.hook: a child who thinks the lighthouse is calling the ships in

facts.fact: When a group needs to pick one thing, people can vote. Each person picks once, and the choice with the most votes wins.
facts.hook: a class voting on a name for the pet fish

facts.fact: When you have a cold, resting in bed or on the couch helps your body get better.
facts.hook: A child wants to run outside while sick, and a grown-up tucks them in with a favourite book instead.

facts.fact: A cold can make your nose runny or stuffy.
facts.hook: A child keeps sniffing during breakfast and learns to ask for a tissue.

facts.fact: After you blow your nose, the used tissue goes in the bin.
facts.hook: A child leaves used tissues on the couch, then makes a game of dropping each one in the bin.

facts.fact: When you cough or sneeze, you cover it with your elbow.
facts.hook: A child sneezes into their hand, then a grandparent shows the elbow trick and they practise it.

facts.fact: Washing your hands with soap and water is a good thing to do after blowing your nose.
facts.hook: A child blows their nose and then reaches for a snack, but remembers to wash hands first.

facts.fact: Only a grown-up gives a child medicine.
facts.hook: A child sees the medicine bottle on the counter and waits for a parent to measure the dose.

facts.fact: A thermometer is a tool a grown-up uses to check how warm your body is.
facts.hook: A child is curious about the thermometer and holds still while a parent checks their temperature.

facts.fact: Drinking water helps when you are sick.
facts.hook: A child doesn't feel thirsty, so a grandparent brings a special cup to make sipping water fun.

facts.fact: A doctor can listen to your chest with a stethoscope.
facts.hook: At the doctor's office, a child is nervous about the stethoscope, then gets to hear the doctor explain it.

facts.fact: At a pharmacy, a pharmacist gives out the medicine a doctor says you need.
facts.hook: A child goes with a parent to the pharmacy and watches the pharmacist hand over the medicine bag.

facts.fact: When you feel sick, you tell a grown-up.
facts.hook: A child feels a sore throat at a grandparent's house and decides to tell Grandma instead of hiding it.

facts.fact: When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much.
facts.hook: A child only wants a few bites of dinner, and a parent says that's okay while they are sick.

facts.fact: We brush our teeth in the morning and before bed.
facts.hook: A child forgets to brush before bed and hops back out of bed to do it.

facts.fact: We wash our hands before we eat.
facts.hook: A child runs to the table with muddy hands and is sent back to the sink first.

facts.fact: Breakfast is the first meal of the day.
facts.hook: A child wants cookies for breakfast and helps choose a morning meal instead.

facts.fact: Socks go on your feet before your shoes.
facts.hook: A child puts shoes on first, then laughs and starts over with socks.

facts.fact: Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in.
facts.hook: A child wants to sleep in their party dress and picks cozy pajamas instead.

facts.fact: A grown-up checks the bath water to make sure it is not too hot before you get in.
facts.hook: A child is eager to jump in the bath and waits while a grown-up tests the water with a hand.

facts.fact: Soap rubbed with water makes bubbles on your hands.
facts.hook: A child makes a bubbly soap beard during handwashing and giggles.

facts.fact: A towel dries your body after a bath.
facts.hook: A child runs off dripping wet and comes back for the towel.

facts.fact: Dirty clothes go in the laundry basket so they can be washed.
facts.hook: A child leaves clothes on the floor, then plays basketball with socks into the laundry basket.

facts.fact: After using the toilet, we flush and then wash our hands.
facts.hook: A child forgets to flush, then remembers both steps on the second try.

facts.fact: Sleeping at night gives your body rest for the next day.
facts.hook: A child wants to stay up late and is too tired to play the next morning, so they go to bed on time.

facts.fact: Brushing or combing your hair gets the tangles out.
facts.hook: A child wakes up with messy hair and brushes it slowly so it doesn't pull.

facts.fact: A teacher is the grown-up who looks after and helps the children in a class.
facts.hook: A child is shy and learns the teacher's name, then feels brave enough to say hello.

facts.fact: Feeling nervous on the first day of school is okay.
facts.hook: A child's tummy feels fluttery at the classroom door, and a parent says they felt that way too.

facts.fact: Writing your name on your things helps them find their way back to you.
facts.hook: Two children have the same lunchbox, and the name on the lid solves the mix-up.

facts.fact: A backpack is a bag you carry on your back.
facts.hook: A child's new backpack is too heavy, so they take out the toys they packed.

facts.fact: If you need help at school, you can ask the teacher.
facts.hook: A child can't find the bathroom and gathers courage to ask the teacher.

facts.fact: On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats.
facts.hook: A child wants to stand and wave out the window, then sits down when the driver asks.

facts.fact: You can make a new friend by telling someone your name and asking theirs.
facts.hook: A child stands alone on the playground, then walks over and asks another child their name.

facts.fact: When a class walks somewhere together, the children often walk in a line.
facts.hook: A child rushes ahead in the hallway and learns to find their spot in the line.

facts.fact: A classroom has rules that everyone in the class follows.
facts.hook: The teacher reads the class rules, and a child reminds a new friend of one later.

facts.fact: At school, children take turns on the playground slide.
facts.hook: A child wants to go down the slide again right away and learns to wait at the back of the line.

facts.fact: A school day has a time for eating a snack or lunch.
facts.hook: A child gets hungry in the morning and learns to wait for snack time with the class.

facts.fact: Red, yellow and blue are called the primary colours.
facts.hook: A child finds only three paint pots and wonders how to paint a whole rainbow.

facts.fact: Mixing yellow paint and blue paint makes green.
facts.hook: A child has no green paint for grass and mixes yellow and blue to make some.

facts.fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange.
facts.hook: A child wants to paint an orange pumpkin and discovers how to mix the colour.

facts.fact: Once two paints are mixed together, you cannot pull them apart again.
facts.hook: A child mixes all the yellow into the blue by accident and learns to keep a little of each aside.

facts.fact: Adding white paint to a colour makes it lighter.
facts.hook: A child's blue sky is too dark, so they stir in some white.

facts.fact: Rinsing your brush in water before a new colour keeps the colours clean.
facts.hook: A child's yellow keeps turning muddy until they remember to rinse the brush.

facts.fact: Wet paint can smudge if you touch it.
facts.hook: A child touches the painting too soon and leaves a fingerprint, then waits for the next one to dry.

facts.fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
facts.hook: A child wants to paint in a new shirt, then puts on a smock first.

facts.fact: A palette is a flat tray or board for holding and mixing paint.
facts.hook: A child mixes paint right on the paper, then tries using a palette to test colours first.

facts.fact: Paintbrushes are washed with water and left to dry when painting is finished.
facts.hook: A child leaves brushes in the paint and finds them stiff the next day, so they wash them this time.

facts.fact: A zipper has two sides that join together when you pull the zipper tab up.
facts.hook: A child's coat hangs open in the wind and they practise pulling the tab up.

facts.fact: To start a zipper, the end of one side slides into the little box at the bottom of the other side.
facts.hook: A child keeps pulling the tab with no luck, until they fit the end into the box first.

facts.fact: Pulling the zipper tab down opens your coat.
facts.hook: A child gets too warm inside the laundromat and unzips their coat by themselves.

facts.fact: One way to put on a coat is to lay it on the floor, put your arms in the sleeves and flip it over your head.
facts.hook: A child struggles to find the second sleeve, and a friend shows them the coat-flip trick.

facts.fact: Each arm goes into its own sleeve of the coat.
facts.hook: A child puts both arms in one sleeve and laughs before trying again.

facts.fact: A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold outside.
facts.hook: A child wants to go to the bus stop without a coat, then feels the cold air and goes back for it.

facts.fact: A hood is the part of a coat you can pull up over your head.
facts.hook: It starts to drizzle at the bus stop, and a child remembers their coat has a hood.

facts.fact: If your shirt gets caught in the zipper, pulling the zipper back down a little can free it.
facts.hook: A child's zipper gets stuck on their sweater, and they learn to back it down gently.

facts.fact: Buttons go through buttonholes to close a coat.
facts.hook: A child's new coat has buttons instead of a zipper, and they practise pushing each through its hole.

facts.fact: Hanging your coat on a hook keeps it off the floor.
facts.hook: A child drops their coat in the hallway and can't find it later, so next time they hang it up.

facts.fact: Pockets in a coat can hold small things like mittens.
facts.hook: A child keeps losing a mitten until they tuck both into their coat pocket.

facts.fact: Learning to zip your own coat takes practice.
facts.hook: A child can't zip up on the first try but keeps practising and finally does it at the bank.

facts.fact: A tablet has a button you press to turn it on.
facts.hook: A child taps the dark screen again and again, then a grown-up shows them the power button.

facts.fact: On a tablet, you tap the screen with your finger to choose things.
facts.hook: A child presses hard with a whole hand, then learns a gentle tap with one finger works.

facts.fact: The small pictures on a tablet screen are called icons, and tapping one opens an app.
facts.hook: A child looks for the drawing app and finds its paintbrush icon.

facts.fact: In a drawing app, moving your finger across the screen draws a line.
facts.hook: A child draws a squiggly line by accident and turns it into a snake.

facts.fact: Holding a tablet with two hands helps keep it from falling.
facts.hook: A child carries the tablet in one hand and almost drops it, then uses both hands.

facts.fact: Tablets are kept away from water and drinks.
facts.hook: A child sets juice beside the tablet, then moves the cup to another table.

facts.fact: Children ask a grown-up before using a tablet.
facts.hook: A child sees Grandpa's tablet on the table and asks him before picking it up.

facts.fact: A tablet runs out of power after being used and needs charging.
facts.hook: The tablet screen goes black in the middle of a drawing, and a grown-up plugs in the charger.

facts.fact: A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall.
facts.hook: A child wants to plug in the tablet and helps by bringing the charger to a grown-up.

facts.fact: Pressing the power button when you are done makes the screen go dark.
facts.hook: A child finishes drawing and presses the button to turn the tablet off before putting it away.

facts.fact: When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place.
facts.hook: A child leaves the tablet on the couch and someone almost sits on it, so they put it on its shelf.

facts.fact: Many drawing apps let you pick a colour by tapping it.
facts.hook: A child wants a red sun and hunts for the red colour to tap.

facts.fact: Children have twenty baby teeth.
facts.hook: A child counts their teeth in the mirror with a parent's help and wonders which will wiggle first.

facts.fact: A tooth that is getting ready to fall out feels wobbly when you touch it with your tongue.
facts.hook: A child at the dinner table notices a tooth moving and announces the news.

facts.fact: Losing baby teeth is a normal part of growing up.
facts.hook: A child is scared when a tooth wiggles, and an older sibling shows the gap from their own lost tooth.

facts.fact: A wobbly tooth is best left to come out on its own or with a grown-up's help, not pulled hard.
facts.hook: A friend on the playground dares a child to yank their tooth, and the child decides to wait instead.

facts.fact: When a baby tooth comes out, there can be a little blood.
facts.hook: A child sees a spot of blood on their napkin, and a grandparent gives them a clean cloth to bite on.

facts.fact: After a tooth falls out, you can feel an empty gap with your tongue.
facts.hook: A child keeps poking the new gap with their tongue and makes funny faces in the mirror.

facts.fact: Grown-up teeth are meant to last the rest of your life.
facts.hook: A child wonders if the new tooth will fall out too and learns it is the one to look after.

facts.fact: In some families, children put a lost tooth under their pillow for the Tooth Fairy.
facts.hook: A child can't find their lost tooth before bedtime and searches the playground with a friend.

facts.fact: A dentist is a doctor who looks after teeth.
facts.hook: At the dental clinic, a child shows the dentist their wobbly tooth.

facts.fact: Biting into hard food can be tricky with a wobbly tooth.
facts.hook: A child tries to bite an apple with a wobbly front tooth, and a parent slices it for them.

facts.fact: You keep brushing gently around a wobbly tooth.
facts.hook: A child wants to skip brushing because of the wobbly tooth, then brushes softly around it.

facts.fact: Opposites are two words that mean things as different as they can be, like big and small.
facts.hook: A child and a friend play a game where one says a word and the other shouts its opposite.

facts.fact: Up and down are opposites.
facts.hook: A child climbs up the playground ladder and slides back down.

facts.fact: A cup with nothing in it is empty, and a cup filled to the top is full.
facts.hook: A child pours water too fast and learns to stop before the cup overflows.

facts.fact: Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut.
facts.hook: A child leaves the fridge open, and a grown-up asks them to close it.

facts.fact: Wet and dry are opposites.
facts.hook: A child splashes a puddle and needs to change into dry socks.

facts.fact: Loud and quiet are opposites.
facts.hook: A child bangs a drum loudly at naptime and switches to a quiet tap.

facts.fact: Day and night are opposites.
facts.hook: A child wakes in the dark, thinks it's morning, and learns it's still night.

facts.fact: Long and short are opposites.
facts.hook: Two children compare their scarves and find one long and one short.

facts.fact: Heavy and light are opposites.
facts.hook: A child tries to lift a heavy box, then carries a light feather pillow easily.

facts.fact: In and out are opposites.
facts.hook: A child keeps putting toys in the box while a baby sibling takes them out.

facts.fact: Pretending means acting as if something is real when it is not.
facts.hook: A child pretends the floor is a river and hops from cushion to cushion.

facts.fact: In pretend play, a cardboard box can become a car, a boat or a house.
facts.hook: A child and a friend argue over what the big box should be and decide to take turns.

facts.fact: When you play house, each person can pick a role, like the parent or the baby.
facts.hook: Two friends both want to be the parent, so they agree to switch halfway.

facts.fact: Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth.
facts.hook: A child makes pinecone soup in the forest and pretends to slurp it without eating it.

facts.fact: You can pretend to take care of a doll or stuffed animal, like feeding it or tucking it into bed.
facts.hook: A child's teddy is 'sick', so they give it pretend medicine and a blanket.

facts.fact: Toys cannot really feel, but you can pretend they do.
facts.hook: A child is upset that they dropped their doll, and a parent says the doll is fine and they can give it a pretend hug.

facts.fact: Saying "Let's pretend" tells your friends a game is starting.
facts.hook: A child wants to play but doesn't know how to start, then says "Let's pretend we're pirates!"

facts.fact: Dress-up clothes help you pretend to be someone else.
facts.hook: A child puts on a big hat and becomes a firefighter for the afternoon.

facts.fact: In a pretend shop, one person can be the shopkeeper and another can be the shopper.
facts.hook: A child runs a pretend shop at the park and learns to wait for a customer to choose.

facts.fact: Friends playing pretend together can agree on what happens next.
facts.hook: One friend says the dragon is friendly and the other says it's scary, so they agree on a friendly dragon.

facts.fact: When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away.
facts.hook: A child leaves the pretend kitchen in a mess, then tidies it with a friend before going home.

facts.fact: A pretend tea party can use empty cups with no real tea in them.
facts.hook: A child pours pretend tea for their stuffed animals and says "Careful, it's pretend hot!"

facts.fact: Taking turns means each person gets a go, one after another.
facts.hook: Two children both want the swing and agree that each gets a turn.

facts.fact: Sharing means letting someone else use something too.
facts.hook: A child has all the crayons, then notices a friend with none and shares some.

facts.fact: We say "please" when we ask for something.
facts.hook: A child grabs for the bread at the dinner table, then remembers to say please.

facts.fact: We say "thank you" when someone gives us something or helps us.
facts.hook: A child forgets to thank Grandma for a gift and goes back to say it.

facts.fact: We ask before we take something that belongs to someone else.
facts.hook: A child takes a friend's toy without asking, sees the friend upset, and gives it back to ask properly.

facts.fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
facts.hook: A child bumps into a friend's block tower and says sorry, then helps rebuild it.

facts.fact: Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn.
facts.hook: A child pushes to the front of the checkout line at the store, then goes back to their spot.

facts.fact: A game has rules that all the players follow.
facts.hook: A child changes the rules in the middle of a game and the others stop playing, so they go back to the real rules.

facts.fact: When someone is talking, we listen and wait until they finish.
facts.hook: A child keeps interrupting at dinner, then practises waiting to share their story.

facts.fact: Being fair means everyone gets a chance.
facts.hook: A child gives all the blocks to one friend and learns to split them so everyone can build.

facts.fact: Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with.
facts.hook: A child walks away from the playroom mess, then comes back to help tidy.

facts.fact: When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice.
facts.hook: A child shouts in Grandpa's house while the baby sleeps and switches to a whisper.

facts.fact: A birthday celebrates the day a person was born.
facts.hook: A child asks why everyone is making a fuss today, and Grandma shows a baby photo from the day they were born.

facts.fact: On your birthday, you turn one year older.
facts.hook: A child who was three yesterday proudly tells everyone at the park that today they are four.

facts.fact: When a birthday cake has candles, a grown-up is the one who lights them.
facts.hook: A child wants to light the candles herself, and Dad explains that lighting is a grown-up job while she gets to make the wish.

facts.fact: If a cake has one candle for each year, a child turning five gets five candles.
facts.hook: A child counts the candles on the cake and notices one is missing, so Mom adds the fifth before it is lit.

facts.fact: Wrapping paper hides a present, so nobody can see what is inside until it is opened.
facts.hook: A child shakes and squeezes a wrapped box trying to guess what is inside, and has to wait until it is opened.

facts.fact: People say thank you when someone gives them a present.
facts.hook: A child rushes to the next present and then remembers to go back and thank the friend who gave the first one.

facts.fact: A party invitation tells guests when and where the party will be.
facts.hook: A friend is worried about getting lost, so a child shows them the invitation that says the party is at the bowling alley.

facts.fact: A balloon blown up with air from a person's breath does not float up to the ceiling.
facts.hook: A child lets go of a balloon Dad blew up, expecting it to fly away, and watches it drift down to the floor instead.

facts.fact: You can show how old you are by holding up that many fingers.
facts.hook: A new friend asks a child's age, and the child holds up four fingers after first accidentally showing three.

facts.fact: When people sing 'Happy Birthday to You,' they sing the birthday person's name in the song.
facts.hook: A shy child hears everyone sing their name in the song and hides a big smile behind their hands.

facts.fact: A shot is a quick poke in the arm or leg with a thin needle.
facts.hook: A child imagines a shot will be huge and scary, then finds it is over with one quick poke in the arm.

facts.fact: Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses.
facts.hook: A child asks why they need a shot when they are not sick, and the doctor explains it helps keep them from getting sick.

facts.fact: The person giving the shot is the only one who handles the needle; children never touch it.
facts.hook: A child wants to hold the needle to see it, and the nurse kindly says only she handles it, but he can hold her sticker sheet.

facts.fact: Used needles go into a special hard box so nobody gets poked.
facts.hook: A child asks what the red box on the wall is for and watches the nurse drop the used needle inside.

facts.fact: A grown-up can hold a child on their lap during a shot to help them feel safe.
facts.hook: A child feels scared on the big table, so Mom sits down and holds him on her lap for the shot.

facts.fact: After a shot, the nurse may put a small bandage over the spot.
facts.hook: A child picks a bandage with stars on it and shows it off at the ice cream shop afterward.

facts.fact: The spot where you got a shot can feel sore for a little while afterward.
facts.hook: A child's arm feels achy in the car on the way home, and Dad says that is okay and it will feel better soon.

facts.fact: A doctor uses a stethoscope to listen to your heart beating.
facts.hook: A child is curious about the tube around the doctor's neck and gets to hear their own heartbeat through it.

facts.fact: A scale at the doctor's office shows how much you weigh.
facts.hook: A child keeps wiggling on the scale and learns to stand still so the number stops jumping.

facts.fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help you feel calmer when you are scared.
facts.hook: A child feels nervous waiting for the shot, and Grandpa helps her breathe in slowly like smelling a flower.

facts.fact: A waiting room is where families sit until it is their turn to see the doctor.
facts.hook: A child is impatient in the waiting room until a nurse calls their name at the door.

facts.fact: A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth.
facts.hook: A child thinks they are going to a regular doctor and is surprised the dentist only wants to look at their teeth.

facts.fact: The dentist's chair tips back so you lie down while the dentist looks in your mouth.
facts.hook: A child giggles in surprise when the big chair slowly leans back like a ride.

facts.fact: A bright light above the dentist's chair helps the dentist see inside your mouth.
facts.hook: A child squints at the bright light, and the dentist hands them sunglasses to wear.

facts.fact: The dentist uses a tiny mirror on a handle to see the backs of your teeth.
facts.hook: A child wonders how the dentist can see behind their teeth and gets to look at the little mirror afterward.

facts.fact: You open your mouth wide so the dentist can see every tooth.
facts.hook: A child keeps closing their mouth to talk, then learns to open wide like a lion's roar.

facts.fact: A dentist wears gloves when putting fingers or tools in your mouth.
facts.hook: A child asks why the dentist's hands are blue and learns they are gloves to keep things clean.

facts.fact: Front teeth are for biting food, and back teeth are for chewing it.
facts.hook: On the bus home, a child bites an apple slice with front teeth and then chomps it with back teeth, like the dentist showed.

facts.fact: After brushing, you spit the toothpaste out instead of swallowing it.
facts.hook: A child is about to swallow the minty foam, then remembers to spit it into the sink.

facts.fact: Each person uses their own toothbrush; people do not share toothbrushes.
facts.hook: A child grabs a sibling's toothbrush by mistake and swaps it back for their own green one.

facts.fact: Soft butter spreads more easily than hard butter straight from the fridge.
facts.hook: A child's toast gets holes from cold, hard butter, so they try again with butter that has sat out and it spreads smoothly.

facts.fact: Spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread.
facts.hook: A child pokes at the toast with the knife tip and makes a mess, then learns to use the flat side.

facts.fact: Toast is bread that has been heated until it turns brown and crunchy.
facts.hook: A child notices the soft white bread came out of the toaster brown and crunchy and asks what happened.

facts.fact: Butter spread on warm toast melts.
facts.hook: A child watches the pat of butter on warm toast turn shiny and melt away and thinks it has disappeared.

facts.fact: Pouring slowly helps keep milk from splashing out of the cup.
facts.hook: A child pours fast and milk splashes on the table, so the next time they pour slowly and it stays in the cup.

facts.fact: Stopping before the cup is full to the top makes it easier to carry without spilling.
facts.hook: A child fills a cup to the very brim and spills while walking, then learns to leave some room at the top.

facts.fact: A small jug is easier for small hands to pour from than a big, heavy carton.
facts.hook: A child struggles with the big milk carton, and Dad pours some into a little jug so they can pour it themselves.

facts.fact: Setting the cup down on the table before pouring keeps it still.
facts.hook: A child tries to hold the cup and pour at the same time, then sets the cup on the table and pours much more neatly.

facts.fact: Milk goes back in the fridge after pouring, to keep it cold.
facts.hook: A child leaves the milk on the counter after breakfast and remembers to put it back in the fridge.

facts.fact: If milk spills, you can wipe it up with a cloth.
facts.hook: A child feels upset about a little puddle of milk, then gets a cloth and wipes it up all by themselves.

facts.fact: The English alphabet has 26 letters.
facts.hook: A child counts the letters on the classroom alphabet chart and is amazed to get all the way to twenty-six.

facts.fact: The alphabet starts with the letter A and ends with the letter Z.
facts.hook: A child thinks the alphabet ends at the letter P until they finish the song and reach Z.

facts.fact: The alphabet song sings the letters in order from A to Z.
facts.hook: A child mixes up the order of the letters and uses the alphabet song to find where M goes.

facts.fact: Letters can be written as big capital letters or small lowercase letters.
facts.hook: A child thinks the small 'a' in a book is a different letter from the big 'A' on the wall, and learns they are the same letter.

facts.fact: A person's name is written with a capital letter at the start.
facts.hook: A child writes their name with a small first letter and then fixes it with a big capital one.

facts.fact: The lowercase letters b and d look alike but face opposite ways.
facts.hook: A child reads 'dog' as 'bog' and giggles, then checks which way the round part of the letter faces.

facts.fact: Sun, sock and sand all start with the letter S and the 'sss' sound.
facts.hook: A child goes on a hunt around the reading nook for things that start with the hissing 'sss' sound.

facts.fact: Tracing a letter's shape with your finger helps you learn how to write it.
facts.hook: A child keeps writing K the wrong way until they trace it with a finger on a bumpy letter card.

facts.fact: Pictures in a book can give clues about what the words say.
facts.hook: A child cannot read the word 'frog' until they look at the picture of a green frog on the lily pad.

facts.fact: Pointing to each word with your finger helps you keep your place while reading.
facts.hook: A child keeps skipping lines until they start moving a finger under each word.

facts.fact: When you reach the end of a line, you go to the start of the next line down.
facts.hook: A child reads a line and then jumps to the wrong place, until Grandpa shows them where the next line starts.

facts.fact: A period at the end of a sentence tells you to stop for a short pause.
facts.hook: A child reads every sentence in one long breath, then learns to pause at each little dot.

facts.fact: A question mark at the end of a sentence shows that someone is asking something.
facts.hook: A child reads a line flatly and then reads it again with their voice going up, like asking a question.

facts.fact: Reading the same book again and again helps its words feel easier to read.
facts.hook: A child struggles through a book on Monday and is surprised how smoothly it goes when they read it again.

facts.fact: If you get stuck on a word, you can ask a grown-up for help.
facts.hook: A child wants to read the whole book alone and feels frustrated at one hard word, then asks the teacher and keeps going.

facts.fact: You can read out loud, or read quietly in your head.
facts.hook: At the library, a child learns to read in a whisper and then silently so they do not disturb others.

facts.fact: A bookmark keeps your place in a book when you stop reading.
facts.hook: A child has to stop reading for dinner and makes a bookmark so they can find their page later.

facts.fact: The last place you remember having something is a good place to start looking.
facts.hook: A child searches everywhere for their bunny, then remembers holding it at snack time and looks by the snack table.

facts.fact: Retracing your steps means going back to each place you went, in order.
facts.hook: A child walks back along the park path, stopping at the swings and the slide, looking for their lost car.

facts.fact: Small toys can roll or slide under furniture like couches and beds.
facts.hook: A child checks the whole room for their marble before thinking to look under the couch.

facts.fact: Things can end up inside other things, like a toy tucked in a bag or coat pocket.
facts.hook: After a long search at Grandma's house, a child finds their toy dinosaur in their own coat pocket.

facts.fact: Searching one room at a time helps you not miss any places.
facts.hook: A child runs from room to room without really looking, then slows down and checks one room at a time.

facts.fact: A flashlight helps you see into dark spots, like under a bed.
facts.hook: A child cannot see anything under the bed until Mom hands them a flashlight.

facts.fact: Asking family to help look means more people are searching.
facts.hook: A child is about to give up, then asks a big sister and Dad to help, and together they find the toy.

facts.fact: If you lose something in a busy place, you tell your grown-up instead of going to search by yourself.
facts.hook: A child realizes their teddy is missing at the park and wants to run off to look, but tells Dad first and they search together.

facts.fact: A lost and found is a place where people put things they find, so the owners can get them back.
facts.hook: A child's hat goes missing at daycare, and the teacher helps them check the lost and found box.

facts.fact: Writing your name on a toy's tag helps people know it belongs to you.
facts.hook: The bus driver finds a toy with a name tag and is able to give it back to the right child.

facts.fact: Putting a toy back in the same place each time makes it easy to find.
facts.hook: After finding their lost toy, a child decides to always keep it in a special basket by the bed.

facts.fact: When you find something that belongs to someone else, you give it back to them.
facts.hook: A child finds a shiny toy car at daycare and wants to keep it, but hands it back to the boy who lost it.

facts.fact: Seeds need water to start growing.
facts.hook: A child plants seeds and forgets to water them, then learns why nothing is happening and gets the watering can.

facts.fact: A tiny new plant poking up out of the soil is called a sprout.
facts.hook: After many days of checking, a child spots a small green sprout and runs to tell everyone.

facts.fact: A plant's roots grow down into the soil.
facts.hook: A child gently pulls up a weed and is surprised by the long stringy roots hanging from the bottom.

facts.fact: A vegetable plant that does not get enough water droops.
facts.hook: A child sees the lettuce drooping on a hot day and gives it a drink from the watering can.

facts.fact: Weeds are plants growing where the gardener does not want them.
facts.hook: A child is about to pull up a baby carrot, thinking it is a weed, and Mom helps them tell the difference.

facts.fact: Peas grow inside pods on the plant.
facts.hook: A child picks a green pod, not sure what it is, and pops it open to find a row of peas inside.

facts.fact: A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot.
facts.hook: A child forgets where the tomatoes were planted, so they make picture labels for every row.

facts.fact: The printed words in a book say the same thing every time the book is read.
facts.hook: A child notices that Mom and Dad both read the exact same words on the page, even though they are different people.

facts.fact: When a grown-up reads a book aloud, they are reading the words, not just looking at the pictures.
facts.hook: A child asks Dad to read a page with no words, and he explains there is nothing written there to read.

facts.fact: A book's title is its name.
facts.hook: A child wants a favorite book from the library shelf and learns to ask for it by its title.

facts.fact: The author is the person who wrote the words of a book.
facts.hook: A child asks who made up the story, and the librarian points to the author's name on the cover.

facts.fact: An illustrator is a person who draws or paints the pictures for a book.
facts.hook: A child loves the pictures in a book and wants to know who drew them, so they find the illustrator's name.

facts.fact: A book in English starts at the front cover, and you turn the pages until you reach the back.
facts.hook: A child opens a book from the back and the story seems all mixed up, so they flip it over to start at the front.

facts.fact: In English, the words on a page are read from left to right.
facts.hook: A child runs a finger from the right side of the page, and the teacher shows them to start from the left.

facts.fact: Some languages, like Arabic and Hebrew, are read from right to left.
facts.hook: A friend at daycare shows a book that opens the other way, and a child learns it is written in Hebrew.

facts.fact: In English, there is a space between one word and the next.
facts.hook: A child writes a note with all the letters squished together, then adds spaces so Grandpa can read it.

facts.fact: Your name written down has the same letters in the same order every time.
facts.hook: A child spots their name on a cubby at daycare and on a birthday card and sees it looks the same both times.

facts.fact: Words are all around us, on signs, labels and boxes, and they tell us things.
facts.hook: At the library, a child notices a sign on the door and asks what the words say.

facts.fact: If you hold a book upside down, the words and pictures look upside down too.
facts.hook: At bedtime, a child pretends to read a book upside down and laughs at the upside-down pictures before turning it around.

facts.fact: Today is the day that is happening right now.
facts.hook: A child asks if today is the day of the library visit, and Mom says yes, it is today.

facts.fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
facts.hook: A child says they went to the park 'tomorrow' and then corrects it to yesterday, because it already happened.

facts.fact: Tomorrow is the day after today.
facts.hook: A child wants to go to a friend's house right now and learns they have to wait until tomorrow, after sleeping.

facts.fact: After you sleep tonight and wake up, today will be called yesterday.
facts.hook: At bedtime, a child wonders where today goes, and Dad explains that tomorrow it will be called yesterday.

facts.fact: Now means at this very moment.
facts.hook: A child asks for a story now, and the teacher says the story is not now, it is after snack.

facts.fact: Later means some time after now, not right away.
facts.hook: A child is told they can play with the blocks later and keeps asking 'is it later yet?'

facts.fact: Soon means in a little while.
facts.hook: A child waiting at the library is told storytime starts soon, and it does not have to be a long wait.

facts.fact: A day goes from morning, to afternoon, to evening, to night.
facts.hook: A child thinks it is morning after a nap, and Grandma explains it is afternoon now.

facts.fact: A week has seven days.
facts.hook: A child counts the days on their fingers to see how long a week is and runs out of one hand.

facts.fact: A clock shows what time it is.
facts.hook: A child keeps asking when it will be time to go, and Mom shows them the clock on the bedroom wall.

facts.fact: When you close your eyes, you cannot see the things around you.
facts.hook: A child covers their eyes during hide-and-seek and thinks nobody can see them, then learns the others still can.

facts.fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes loud sounds quieter.
facts.hook: A noisy blender startles a child in the kitchen, and they cover their ears until it stops.

facts.fact: Your tongue can taste that a lemon is sour.
facts.hook: A child expects a lemon slice at dinner to taste sweet like orange juice and scrunches up their face.

facts.fact: You can often smell dinner cooking before you see it.
facts.hook: A child playing in another room guesses what is for dinner just by sniffing the air.

facts.fact: Your fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy.
facts.hook: A child plays a guessing game with eyes closed, feeling a pinecone, a feather and a smooth stone.

facts.fact: Your nose has two openings called nostrils.
facts.hook: A child looks in a mirror to count the openings in their nose after a grown-up names them.

facts.fact: Holding your nose closed makes food taste less strong.
facts.hook: A child tries holding their nose while eating a strawberry and is surprised how plain it tastes.

facts.fact: Eyelashes help keep dust and bits of dirt out of your eyes.
facts.hook: A child wonders why they have eyelashes after a windy day at the park.

facts.fact: An ice cube feels cold when you touch it.
facts.hook: A child holds an ice cube at the table and quickly drops it into their cup because it feels so cold.

facts.fact: Glasses help some people see more clearly.
facts.hook: A child tries to understand why Grandpa puts on his glasses before reading a story.

facts.fact: Your feet can feel things too, like soft grass under bare toes.
facts.hook: A child takes off their shoes in the backyard and describes how the grass tickles their feet.

facts.fact: It is hard to see in the dark, so we turn on a light.
facts.hook: A child cannot find their teddy in a dark room until a grown-up switches on the lamp.

facts.fact: Mixing blue paint and yellow paint makes green.
facts.hook: A child needs green for grass but has only blue and yellow paint, so they mix them.

facts.fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange.
facts.hook: A child wants to paint a pumpkin but there is no orange paint in the jar.

facts.fact: Wet glue needs time to dry before the pieces hold together.
facts.hook: A child lifts a paper crown too soon and the pieces slide apart, so they wait and try again.

facts.fact: Children cut paper with rounded-tip safety scissors while a grown-up watches.
facts.hook: A child asks for the big scissors, and the grown-up hands them the child-size safety scissors instead.

facts.fact: Crayons can melt if they are left in a hot car on a sunny day.
facts.hook: A child finds a box of crayons gone soft and bendy after leaving it in the family car.

facts.fact: Washable markers wash off skin with soap and water.
facts.hook: A child draws on their own hand by mistake and worries until soap and water wash it away.

facts.fact: Wet paint smears if you touch it before it dries.
facts.hook: A child touches a painting too soon and smudges the sun, then learns to wait.

facts.fact: If you paint on one half of a paper and fold it while the paint is wet, the paint prints onto the other half.
facts.hook: A child makes a butterfly by folding painted paper and opening it to find two matching wings.

facts.fact: People often write their name on their artwork so everyone knows who made it.
facts.hook: Two children at the library make almost the same drawing and cannot tell whose is whose.

facts.fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
facts.hook: A child forgets their apron at art class and gets paint on a favorite shirt.

facts.fact: After painting, brushes get rinsed clean so the paint does not dry on them.
facts.hook: A child leaves a brush in the paint and finds it stiff the next day.

facts.fact: A pencil point can break if you press down very hard.
facts.hook: A child presses so hard while drawing that the pencil tip snaps, and they learn to press gently.

facts.fact: Cutting hair does not hurt.
facts.hook: A child is scared the scissors will hurt, and a grown-up shows them it feels like nothing at all.

facts.fact: Hair grows back after it is cut.
facts.hook: A child worries they will lose their hair forever, and a parent explains it grows back.

facts.fact: The hairdresser puts a cape around your shoulders to keep cut hair off your clothes.
facts.hook: A child giggles at the cape and pretends to be a superhero while the hairdresser works.

facts.fact: Sitting very still helps the hairdresser cut your hair neatly.
facts.hook: A child keeps turning to look at the fish tank, then learns to sit still like a statue.

facts.fact: Tiny bits of cut hair can feel itchy on your neck.
facts.hook: A child squirms because their neck itches, and the hairdresser brushes the hairs away.

facts.fact: Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut to remember it.
facts.hook: A parent tucks a little curl into an envelope, and the child asks why.

facts.fact: A hairdresser can hold up a hand mirror to show you the back of your hair.
facts.hook: A child wants to see the back of their new haircut and cannot, until the hairdresser brings a mirror.

facts.fact: A hairdresser uses a comb to keep hair neat while cutting it.
facts.hook: A child counts how many times the hairdresser combs before each snip.

facts.fact: Small children sometimes sit on a booster seat so the hairdresser can reach their hair.
facts.hook: A child is too short for the big chair, so the hairdresser brings a booster seat.

facts.fact: A map is a drawing of a place as if you were looking down on it from above.
facts.hook: A child draws their bed from the side, then remembers a map shows things from above.

facts.fact: A map key shows what each small picture or color on the map means.
facts.hook: A friend cannot tell what the little squares on a map mean until the child adds a key.

facts.fact: Things on a map are drawn much smaller than they really are.
facts.hook: A child tries to draw their bedroom at real size and runs out of paper.

facts.fact: On a map, things that are next to each other in a room are drawn next to each other.
facts.hook: A child draws the toy box far from the bed, then fixes it so it sits right beside the bed.

facts.fact: Looking down from above, a round table looks like a circle.
facts.hook: A child is unsure how to draw the round table until they look down at a round plate and see a circle.

facts.fact: A map can help a person find their way to a place they have not been before.
facts.hook: A cousin visiting Grandma's house uses the child's map to find the bathroom.

facts.fact: Map makers often color water blue.
facts.hook: A child draws the fish tank on their classroom map and picks a blue crayon for it.

facts.fact: On many maps, an arrow with the letter N points north.
facts.hook: A child sees an N arrow on a map at the airport and asks what it means.

facts.fact: People can draw an X on a map to mark a special spot.
facts.hook: A child hides a toy and draws an X on their map so a sibling can find it.

facts.fact: A globe is a round map of the whole Earth.
facts.hook: A child spins a globe at Grandpa's house and looks for where they live.

facts.fact: Turning a map so it matches the way you are facing makes it easier to use.
facts.hook: A child holds their map upside down and gets mixed up in the classroom, then turns it around.

facts.fact: A title like 'My Bedroom' tells people which place a map shows.
facts.hook: A child's map gets mixed up with a friend's, so they write a title on top.

facts.fact: Many families say a blessing or a thank-you before they start eating.
facts.hook: A child starts eating at Grandma's house and then notices everyone else is waiting to say a blessing.

facts.fact: In many families, everyone waits until the blessing is finished before eating.
facts.hook: A hungry child reaches for bread early, then puts it down and waits for the blessing to end.

facts.fact: Some families hold hands around the table while they say a blessing.
facts.hook: A child is holding a spoon when the family reaches for hands, so they set it down to join in.

facts.fact: Some people close their eyes or bow their heads during a blessing.
facts.hook: A child peeks during the blessing and sees Grandpa's eyes closed and head bowed.

facts.fact: A blessing before a meal often says thank you for the food.
facts.hook: A child thinks about who grew the food and adds a thank-you to the family blessing.

facts.fact: Many Jewish families say a blessing called the Hamotzi over bread before a meal.
facts.hook: A child practices the Hamotzi so they can say it over the bread at a family dinner.

facts.fact: Many Christian families say grace, a short prayer of thanks, before meals.
facts.hook: A child visiting a friend's home is asked if they would like to say grace.

facts.fact: Many Muslims say 'Bismillah,' which means 'in the name of God,' before they eat.
facts.hook: A child forgets to say Bismillah, remembers, and says it before the first bite.

facts.fact: In Japan, people say 'itadakimasu' before eating to give thanks for the food.
facts.hook: A child learns to say itadakimasu from a grandparent and tries to say it just right.

facts.fact: In France, people often say 'bon appétit' before a meal to wish everyone a good meal.
facts.hook: A child at a community dinner hears 'bon appétit' and asks what it means.

facts.fact: Some families sing their blessing instead of speaking it.
facts.hook: A child wants to lead the sung blessing but mixes up the tune and tries again.

facts.fact: Many prayers end with the word 'Amen.'
facts.hook: A child waits for the word Amen to know when the blessing is over.

facts.fact: A grown-up must always watch children when they are in or near water.
facts.hook: A child wants to jump in before the teacher arrives, and waits at the side until a grown-up is watching.

facts.fact: Wet floors around a pool are slippery, so people walk instead of run.
facts.hook: A child starts running to the pool, and a grown-up reminds them to walk.

facts.fact: Swim teachers often have children practice blowing bubbles into the water through their mouth.
facts.hook: A child is shy about putting their face near the water, then makes big bubbles and laughs.

facts.fact: Many pools have a shallow end and a deep end.
facts.hook: A child wants to go to the deep end like their big sister, and the teacher explains why they start in the shallow end.

facts.fact: A swim teacher may hold a child while the child learns to float on their back.
facts.hook: A child is nervous about floating until the teacher's hands support their back.

facts.fact: A lifeguard's job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it.
facts.hook: A child wonders why the lifeguard sits up high and learns it helps them see everyone.

facts.fact: Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in.
facts.hook: A child heads straight from the changing room to the pool and is reminded to shower first.

facts.fact: Pool steps or a ladder help you get in and out of the water.
facts.hook: A child tries to climb out over the edge and finds the ladder much easier.

facts.fact: Holding onto the edge of the pool, children can practice kicking their legs.
facts.hook: A child holds the wall and kicks so hard they splash the teacher.

facts.fact: People write on moving boxes to show what is inside or which room it goes in.
facts.hook: A child cannot find their toys in a pile of boxes until they spot the one labeled with their name.

facts.fact: A moving truck carries a family's furniture and boxes to their new home.
facts.hook: A child watches their bed get loaded into the moving truck and worries it will not come back.

facts.fact: You can keep in touch with old friends by video calls, letters or phone calls.
facts.hook: A child misses a best friend and makes a video call to show their new room.

facts.fact: Your favorite things can be packed and taken to your new home.
facts.hook: A child is afraid their teddy will be left behind and packs it in a special box.

facts.fact: Empty rooms can make an echo when you talk or clap.
facts.hook: A child claps in the empty new apartment and hears the sound bounce back.

facts.fact: Saying hello and asking someone's name is a way to start making a new friend.
facts.hook: A shy child in a new classroom practices saying hello before trying it with a classmate.

facts.fact: It is okay to feel sad about leaving old friends.
facts.hook: A child feels sad on moving day and a grown-up tells them it is okay to feel that way.

facts.fact: Some families take photos of their old home to help them remember it.
facts.hook: A child takes a last photo of the old front door before leaving.

facts.fact: A new town can have new places to explore, like a park or a library.
facts.hook: A child who misses the old park discovers a new one down the street.

facts.fact: Neighbors are the people who live near your home.
facts.hook: A child meets a neighbor in the hallway of their new apartment building.

facts.fact: Unpacking takes time, so some things stay in boxes for a while.
facts.hook: A child cannot find their favorite cup on the first night and has to wait until it is unpacked.

facts.fact: On a piano, keys on the left make low sounds and keys on the right make high sounds.
facts.hook: A child wants to play a growly bear sound and has to find which side of the piano to use.

facts.fact: Hitting a drum harder makes a louder sound.
facts.hook: A child bangs the drum so loudly the baby wakes, and learns to tap more softly.

facts.fact: You play a guitar by plucking or strumming its strings.
facts.hook: A child tries to play a guitar by tapping it like a drum, then learns to strum.

facts.fact: Practicing a little every day helps you get better at playing.
facts.hook: A child is frustrated that a song is hard, then keeps practicing and plays it all the way through.

facts.fact: A violin can be played by pulling a bow across its strings.
facts.hook: A child holds the bow the wrong way and makes a squeak, then the teacher shows them how.

facts.fact: Covering different holes on a recorder makes different notes.
facts.hook: A child's recorder squeaks because a finger is not covering its hole all the way.

facts.fact: Written music uses marks called notes to show which sounds to play.
facts.hook: A child sees the dots and lines on a music sheet and asks what they mean.

facts.fact: Musicians keep a steady beat so they can play together.
facts.hook: Two children play together but keep going too fast until they tap a steady beat first.

facts.fact: A piano has black keys and white keys.
facts.hook: A child plays only the black keys and finds they can still make a tune.

facts.fact: String instruments like guitars and violins need tuning so their notes sound right.
facts.hook: A child's guitar sounds funny, and the teacher turns the pegs to tune it.

facts.fact: A music teacher shows you how to hold your instrument.
facts.hook: A child holds the violin upside down at their first lesson until the teacher helps.

facts.fact: After playing for an audience, musicians often bow when people clap.
facts.hook: A child finishes playing at a school concert and forgets to bow, then remembers.

facts.fact: Families often gather together to celebrate special holidays.
facts.hook: A child is excited to see cousins they have not seen in a long time at a family celebration.

facts.fact: Many celebrations have special foods made just for that day.
facts.hook: A child helps a grandparent make a special holiday dish and wants to taste it early.

facts.fact: Many celebrations use candles or lamps, and grown-ups light and handle the flames.
facts.hook: A child wants to light a candle, and a grown-up lets them choose which one while the grown-up does the lighting.

facts.fact: During Diwali, many families light small clay oil lamps called diyas.
facts.hook: A child helps set out unlit diyas in a row, and a grown-up lights them.

facts.fact: During Hanukkah, Jewish families light candles on a menorah for eight nights.
facts.hook: A child counts the lit candles each night of Hanukkah as a grown-up lights one more.

facts.fact: At Lunar New Year, many children receive red envelopes with money inside.
facts.hook: A child gets a red envelope and learns to say thank you before opening it.

facts.fact: People often wear special clothes to a celebration.
facts.hook: A child cannot decide what to wear and then chooses a special outfit for the festival.

facts.fact: Music and dancing are part of many celebrations.
facts.hook: A shy child watches the dancing at a cultural center, then joins in holding a grown-up's hand.

facts.fact: At Christmas, many families decorate a tree.
facts.hook: A child wants to hang every ornament on one branch, then spreads them out.

facts.fact: On Eid, many Muslims greet each other by saying 'Eid Mubarak.'
facts.hook: A child practices saying 'Eid Mubarak' to greet relatives at the door.

facts.fact: At Lunar New Year, lion dancers move to the beat of loud drums.
facts.hook: A child is startled by the loud drums at a street festival, then claps along with the lion dance.

facts.fact: At a big crowded celebration, children stay close to their grown-up.
facts.hook: A child drifts toward a food stall at a street festival, then remembers to hold a grown-up's hand.

facts.fact: Each team wears its own colors so you can tell the two teams apart.
facts.hook: A child cannot tell which team is which until a grown-up points out the uniform colors.

facts.fact: Fans cheer and clap when their team scores.
facts.hook: A child cheers loudly for the wrong team and laughs when they figure it out.

facts.fact: A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules.
facts.hook: A child wonders who the person in the striped shirt is and why they keep watching.

facts.fact: A scoreboard shows how many points each team has.
facts.hook: A child cannot remember the score and learns to look at the scoreboard.

facts.fact: In soccer, a team scores a goal by getting the ball into the other team's net.
facts.hook: A child watching soccer thinks the ball has to go over the net, then learns it goes in.

facts.fact: In basketball, players score by throwing the ball through a hoop.
facts.hook: A child wants to try throwing a ball through the hoop after watching the game.

facts.fact: Fans often wear their team's colors to show which team they cheer for.
facts.hook: A child wants to wear a shirt in their favorite team's colors before the big game.

facts.fact: In ice hockey, players use sticks to hit a flat disc called a puck.
facts.hook: A child at the ice rink keeps looking for a ball, then spots the puck.

facts.fact: In games like soccer and basketball, the team with more points at the end wins.
facts.hook: A child thinks the team that ran more wins, then checks the score.

facts.fact: When both teams have the same score, it is called a tie.
facts.hook: A child asks who won, and a grown-up explains the score is a tie.

facts.fact: In soccer and basketball, the referee blows a whistle to stop play.
facts.hook: A child hears the whistle and wonders why all the players stopped running.

facts.fact: A week has seven days.
facts.hook: A child counts the sleeps until a party and learns the week has seven days, starting again after Sunday.

facts.fact: A year has twelve months.
facts.hook: A child asks how long until their next birthday, and Grandma turns through all twelve months on the calendar.

facts.fact: The days of the week always come in the same order, over and over.
facts.hook: A child thinks Friday comes right after Monday and checks the calendar to find the days in between.

facts.fact: Tomorrow is the day that comes after today.
facts.hook: A child wants the zoo trip now, and Dad explains it is tomorrow, after one more sleep.

facts.fact: Yesterday is the day that came just before today.
facts.hook: A child mixes up yesterday and tomorrow while telling about a library visit, then fixes it.

facts.fact: January is the first month of the year.
facts.hook: A child opens the new calendar to the first page and reads January with a grown-up.

facts.fact: December is the last month of the year.
facts.hook: A child finds the last page of the calendar and sees December.

facts.fact: In English, the name of every day of the week ends in "day".
facts.hook: A child notices Monday and Sunday end the same way and hunts through the other day names.

facts.fact: People write special days on a calendar so they remember when they happen.
facts.hook: A child wants to remember a friend's birthday and helps write it in the right box.

facts.fact: Crossing off each day on a calendar helps you see how many days are left until a special day.
facts.hook: A child crosses off one box each morning to count down to Grandpa's visit.

facts.fact: Each month has its own name, like March or July.
facts.hook: A child learns the name of their birthday month and looks for it on the calendar.

facts.fact: The date is the number that tells which day of the month it is.
facts.hook: At school a child gets to put up today's date number on the class calendar.

facts.fact: Feelings can show on your face, like a big smile when you are happy.
facts.hook: A child looks in a mirror and makes a happy face, then a sad face.

facts.fact: When people feel sad, they sometimes cry.
facts.hook: A child sees a friend crying at daycare and brings a favorite toy to share.

facts.fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help your body calm down when you feel angry.
facts.hook: A child stomps off angry, then tries slow breaths with a grown-up and feels calmer.

facts.fact: Saying how you feel, like "I feel sad," helps grown-ups know how to help you.
facts.hook: A child sulks at the store until they tell Mom, "I feel sad," and she can help.

facts.fact: Feelings change, so a sad feeling can turn into a happy one later.
facts.hook: A child is sad when rain cancels the park, then happy building a blanket fort.

facts.fact: Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups.
facts.hook: A child is surprised to hear Dad felt nervous too, and they talk about it.

facts.fact: When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help.
facts.hook: A child is scared of a noise at bedtime and calls a parent, who helps find the sound.

facts.fact: When you feel excited, you might want to jump, bounce or shout.
facts.hook: A child bounces so much waiting for a visitor that they have to find a calm way to wait.

facts.fact: You can often tell how a friend feels by looking at their face.
facts.hook: A child notices a friend's frown at the library and asks what is wrong.

facts.fact: Two people can feel differently about the same thing.
facts.hook: A child loves the loud drum but a friend covers their ears, so they find a quieter game.

facts.fact: Asking "Are you okay?" shows someone you care about how they feel.
facts.hook: A child sees a friend trip and walks over to ask, "Are you okay?"

facts.fact: Before a concert, performers practice their songs many times so they remember them.
facts.hook: A child keeps forgetting a line and practices it again and again at home.

facts.fact: Feeling nervous before going on stage is a feeling lots of performers have.
facts.hook: A child backstage has a fluttery tummy, and a friend says they feel it too.

facts.fact: The audience claps at the end of a song to show they enjoyed it.
facts.hook: A child thinks the clapping means something went wrong, then learns it means people liked it.

facts.fact: A bow is a way performers say thank you when the audience claps.
facts.hook: A child forgets to bow, sees the others bowing, and quickly joins in.

facts.fact: During a concert, the audience sits and listens while the performers sing.
facts.hook: A child watching another class sing learns to sit quietly until it is their turn.

facts.fact: Backstage is the space behind or beside the stage where performers wait out of sight.
facts.hook: A child peeks out from backstage to spot their family before it is their turn.

facts.fact: A microphone makes a voice louder so everyone in the room can hear.
facts.hook: A child is startled to hear their own voice so loud through the microphone, then smiles.

facts.fact: If you forget a word while singing, you can keep going and join back in.
facts.hook: A child forgets a word, keeps smiling, and joins the song again at the next line.

facts.fact: Bright stage lights can make it hard to see faces in the audience.
facts.hook: A child can't find their family past the bright lights but waves anyway.

facts.fact: Taking slow breaths before going on stage can help calm nervous feelings.
facts.hook: A child's knees wobble before the show, and the teacher breathes slowly with them.

facts.fact: We wash our hands before we eat.
facts.hook: A child reaches for a snack at Grandma's, remembers, and goes to wash first.

facts.fact: We always wash our hands after using the toilet.
facts.hook: A child rushes out of the bathroom to play, then turns back to wash.

facts.fact: Rubbing soap and water on your hands makes bubbles.
facts.hook: A child forgets the soap, sees there are no bubbles, and tries again.

facts.fact: Rinsing under the water washes the soap off your hands.
facts.hook: A child's hands are still slippery with soap, so they rinse again.

facts.fact: Drying your hands with a clean towel is the last step of handwashing.
facts.hook: A child shakes wet hands and drips everywhere, then finds the towel.

facts.fact: Hands that look clean still need washing before eating.
facts.hook: A child says, "My hands aren't dirty!" and learns to wash them anyway.

facts.fact: Health experts say to scrub your hands with soap for at least twenty seconds.
