facts.hook: A child rinses too fast, so they count slowly while scrubbing to keep going longer.

facts.fact: Singing a song while you scrub helps you keep washing long enough.
facts.hook: At summer camp a child learns a handwashing song to sing at the sink.

facts.fact: A grown-up should check that the water is warm, not hot, before you wash.
facts.hook: A child waits for a grown-up to test the tap water before putting hands in.

facts.fact: After playing outside or petting an animal, it is time to wash your hands.
facts.hook: A child pets the dog and then heads to the sink before lunch.

facts.fact: A step stool can help a small child reach the sink, with a grown-up nearby.
facts.hook: A child can't reach the sink at Grandpa's, so Grandpa brings the step stool and stays close.

facts.fact: We see with our eyes.
facts.hook: A child covers their eyes at the park, then opens them and names what they see.

facts.fact: We hear with our ears.
facts.hook: A child sits still in the backyard and lists every sound their ears can hear.

facts.fact: We smell with our nose.
facts.hook: A child sniffs flowers at the park to find which one smells sweetest.

facts.fact: We taste with our tongue.
facts.hook: A child tastes a lemon slice and a strawberry and says which is sour.

facts.fact: We feel things by touching them with our skin, like our fingertips.
facts.hook: A child feels sand, a shell and a stick at the beach and names each feel.

facts.fact: There are five senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching.
facts.hook: A child counts the senses on one hand, forgets one, then remembers.

facts.fact: Pinching your nose shut makes it hard to smell anything.
facts.hook: A child pinches their nose near the cookies and finds they can't smell them.

facts.fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes sounds seem quieter.
facts.hook: A child covers their ears when a truck rumbles by and notices how much quieter it gets.

facts.fact: Your tongue can tell sweet foods from sour ones.
facts.hook: A child guesses sweet or sour for each snack at school.

facts.fact: Your skin can feel whether something is soft or rough.
facts.hook: A child sorts a feather, a pinecone and a blanket into soft and rough.

facts.fact: Your nose can smell some things, like cookies baking, before you can see them.
facts.hook: A child smells cookies from another room and follows their nose to the kitchen.

facts.fact: Never look straight at the sun, because it can hurt your eyes.
facts.hook: A child wants to see the sun up close, and a grown-up explains why not to look at it.

facts.fact: A good pencil grip pinches the pencil between your thumb and first finger, resting it on your middle finger.
facts.hook: A child grips the pencil in a fist, then a grown-up shows the pinch-and-rest way.

facts.fact: In English, we write from left to right across the page.
facts.hook: A child starts their name at the right edge and runs out of room, then starts on the left.

facts.fact: The letters of your name always go in the same order.
facts.hook: A child mixes up two letters in their name and checks the name card to fix it.

facts.fact: An eraser can rub out a pencil mark you want to fix.
facts.hook: A child makes a wobbly letter and uses an eraser to try again.

facts.fact: Pressing too hard on a pencil can break its tip.
facts.hook: A child presses so hard the tip snaps, and learns to press more gently.

facts.fact: Holding the paper still with your other hand helps keep it from sliding.
facts.hook: A child's paper keeps slipping at the library until they hold it with their other hand.

facts.fact: Tracing over dotted letters is one way to practice making letter shapes.
facts.hook: A child traces the dotted letters of their name at Grandma's table.

facts.fact: Some letters are made of straight lines, like L, and some have curves, like O.
facts.hook: A child sorts the letters of their name into straight ones and curvy ones.

facts.fact: A pencil needs sharpening when its tip gets dull, and a grown-up can help.
facts.hook: A child's lines get fat and fuzzy, so they ask a grown-up to sharpen the pencil.

facts.fact: Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone.
facts.hook: A child waves a pencil while walking, then remembers to hold the point down.

facts.fact: Practicing your name many times makes the letters easier to write.
facts.hook: A child writes their name each day and sees it getting neater.

facts.fact: A new baby cannot talk yet, so it cries to show it needs something.
facts.hook: A child wonders why the baby cries so much and learns the baby is asking for help.

facts.fact: A newborn baby drinks milk or formula, not regular food.
facts.hook: A child tries to share a cracker with the baby, and a grown-up explains babies only drink milk.

facts.fact: A newborn cannot hold up its own head, so grown-ups hold the baby's head when they carry it.
facts.hook: A child watches Mom hold the baby's head and asks why.

facts.fact: A big brother or sister can hold a new baby while sitting down, with a grown-up helping.
facts.hook: A child wants to hold the baby, so they sit on the couch with a grown-up right beside them.

facts.fact: Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet.
facts.hook: A child at the baby store asks why the baby needs so many diapers.

facts.fact: New babies sleep for much of the day.
facts.hook: A child wants the baby to play, but the baby is sleeping again.

facts.fact: A new baby will often hold tight to a finger placed in its hand.
facts.hook: A child puts a finger in the baby's hand and feels the baby hold on.

facts.fact: Big brothers and sisters wash their hands before holding a new baby.
facts.hook: A child rushes in from the yard to hold the baby, then washes hands first.

facts.fact: A new baby must be touched very gently.
facts.hook: A child pats the baby too hard, then learns to stroke the baby's hand softly.

facts.fact: Grown-ups feed a new baby many times, both day and night.
facts.hook: A child hears the baby wake up at night and learns it's feeding time again.

facts.fact: Big brothers and sisters can help by fetching things, like a clean diaper.
facts.hook: A child feels left out until they are asked to bring a diaper and a blanket.

facts.fact: It is okay for a big brother or sister to feel left out when a new baby arrives.
facts.hook: In the car a child says they miss having Mom to themselves, and Mom listens.

facts.fact: A coach teaches the team and helps the players learn the game.
facts.hook: A child doesn't know where to stand, and the coach shows them.

facts.fact: A season is all the practices and games a team plays from start to end.
facts.hook: A child asks when the season ends, and the family counts the games left on the schedule.

facts.fact: Practice is when a team learns skills and gets ready for games.
facts.hook: A child wants to skip practice, then sees how practice helped them catch the ball.

facts.fact: Players on a team often wear matching shirts so they can tell who is on their team.
facts.hook: A child passes to the wrong color shirt, then looks for their own team's color.

facts.fact: Players drink water during breaks, especially on hot days.
facts.hook: A child forgets the water bottle on a hot day, and a grown-up brings one over.

facts.fact: In baseball, the batter wears a helmet to protect their head.
facts.hook: A child runs to bat without a helmet, and the coach calls them back to put it on.

facts.fact: In soccer, a team scores by getting the ball into the other team's goal.
facts.hook: A child kicks toward their own goal by mistake, then turns around.

facts.fact: In basketball, a team scores by getting the ball through the hoop.
facts.hook: A child keeps missing the hoop and practices shots in the backyard.

facts.fact: A referee or umpire is the person who makes sure players follow the rules.
facts.hook: A child is upset at a call, and the coach explains the umpire's job.

facts.fact: Teams warm up by running or stretching before a game.
facts.hook: A child wants to start the game right away but joins the warm-up first.

facts.fact: After a game, players often tell the other team "good game."
facts.hook: A child is grumpy after losing, then lines up to say good game.

facts.fact: Teammates can cheer for each other, even when someone misses.
facts.hook: A child misses the ball and hears the team cheer them on to try again.

facts.fact: A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot, so only grown-ups touch it.
facts.hook: A child wonders if the stove is still hot and asks a grown-up instead of touching it.

facts.fact: Steam from a pot or kettle is hot and can burn, so stay back.
facts.hook: A child wants to see the bubbles in the pot and watches from a safe distance with a grown-up.

facts.fact: A grown-up should check that bath water is warm, not hot, before you get in.
facts.hook: A child wants to jump into the bath but waits for a grown-up to test the water.

facts.fact: Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out.
facts.hook: A child heads for the far end of the playground, then comes back when they can't see Dad.

facts.fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
facts.hook: A child loses sight of Mom and goes to the checkout worker for help.

facts.fact: Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street.
facts.hook: A child sees the park across the road and waits to take a grown-up's hand.

facts.fact: Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.
facts.hook: A child notices an outlet behind the couch and tells a grown-up instead of touching it.

facts.fact: Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.
facts.hook: A child finds colorful pills on a table and tells a grown-up without touching them.

facts.fact: Wear a helmet when you ride a bike.
facts.hook: A child wants to ride right away, then goes back for the helmet.

facts.fact: At the playground, go down the slide feet first.
facts.hook: A child starts to lie down head first on the slide, then turns around to go feet first.

facts.fact: Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.
facts.hook: A child sees a lighter in the yard and tells a grown-up without picking it up.

facts.fact: On a rainy day, a raincoat helps keep your body dry.
facts.hook: A child runs out without a raincoat and comes back to put it on.

facts.fact: Rain boots keep your feet dry when you step in puddles.
facts.hook: A child wears sneakers in the rain and ends up with soggy socks.

facts.fact: Rain makes puddles on the ground.
facts.hook: A child finds a big puddle at the playground after the rain.

facts.fact: An umbrella keeps rain off your head.
facts.hook: A child and a grown-up share one umbrella on the walk to school.

facts.fact: On a snowy day, mittens or gloves keep your hands warm.
facts.hook: A child forgets mittens and has cold hands after making a snowball.

facts.fact: Snow melts into water when you bring it inside where it is warm.
facts.hook: A child brings a snowball inside to keep and finds a puddle later.

facts.fact: On a sunny day, a sun hat helps shade your face.
facts.hook: A child squints at the playground until they put on a sun hat.

facts.fact: Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn.
facts.hook: A child wants to rush outside but stops for a grown-up to put on sunscreen.

facts.fact: On a windy day, you can see trees sway and leaves blow around.
facts.hook: A child watches leaves blow across the yard and chases them.

facts.fact: A strong wind can blow a hat right off your head.
facts.hook: A child's hat blows away on a windy day and they chase it across the grass.

facts.fact: On a cloudy day, clouds can hide the sun.
facts.hook: A child waits by the window for the sun to come out from behind the clouds.

facts.fact: When you hear thunder, go indoors.
facts.hook: A child wants to keep playing when thunder rumbles, and a grown-up brings everyone inside.

facts.fact: Mixing blue paint and yellow paint makes green paint.
facts.hook: A child needs green for grass in a painting but the green pot is empty, so she mixes the blue and yellow.

facts.fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
facts.hook: A child wants to paint a pumpkin but has no orange, and a friend shows him which two colors to stir together.

facts.fact: Adding white paint to a color makes it lighter, so red with white becomes pink.
facts.hook: A child wants a pink flower for Grandma's card and discovers it by stirring white into red.

facts.fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
facts.hook: Two children argue over whether a navy crayon is blue, then line up all the blues from lightest to darkest.

facts.fact: On a traffic light, red means stop and green means go.
facts.hook: Holding a grown-up's hand at the crossing, a child calls out each color and what the cars must do.

facts.fact: On a clear, sunny day, the sky looks blue.
facts.hook: A child picks a gray crayon for the sky, looks out the window at the sunny day and swaps it for blue.

facts.fact: Freshly fallen snow is white.
facts.hook: A child wants to draw snow on white paper and wonders how to make white show up, so she uses blue paper instead.

facts.fact: In a very dark room, it is hard to tell what color things are.
facts.hook: A child picks socks in the dark at bedtime and in the morning light finds one red and one green.

facts.fact: Sorting by color means putting all the things that are the same color together in one group.
facts.hook: At clean-up time a child makes a red pile, a blue pile and a yellow pile of blocks, then finds one block hiding in the wrong pile.

facts.fact: You see colors with your eyes; you cannot tell a color by feeling it with your fingers.
facts.hook: Playing a feely-bag game, a child guesses 'red ball!' and finds she can feel it is a ball but must look to see its color.

facts.fact: Families pack clothes that fit the weather where they are going, like a swimsuit for the beach or a warm coat for the snow.
facts.hook: A child packs a swimsuit for a snowy mountain trip and a grown-up helps him find his mittens instead.

facts.fact: At an airport, carry-on bags ride through a machine that checks what is inside them.
facts.hook: A child worries her teddy bear is lost when her backpack disappears into the machine, then cheers when it comes out the other end.

facts.fact: In the car, a young child rides buckled into a car seat to stay safe.
facts.hook: Excited to leave, a child climbs in and forgets to buckle, so the car waits until the click is heard.

facts.fact: A map shows roads and places, so people can find the way somewhere new.
facts.hook: The family takes a wrong turn, and a child helps a grown-up look at the map to find the road again.

facts.fact: On a long drive, the family can stop at a rest stop so people can use the bathroom and stretch.
facts.hook: A child needs the bathroom halfway through the drive and is relieved when the car pulls into a rest stop.

facts.fact: On an airplane, people in their seats buckle their seat belts for takeoff and landing.
facts.hook: A child wants to look out the window standing up, and learns why everyone stays buckled as the plane lifts off.

facts.fact: In busy places like airports, children stay close to their grown-up and hold hands.
facts.hook: A child wants to run to see the big planes, then remembers to hold a grown-up's hand in the crowd.

facts.fact: Taking photos on a trip lets a family remember it after they get home.
facts.hook: Back home, a child misses the beach, so the family looks at their trip photos together.

facts.fact: At the beach, a child goes near the water only with a grown-up watching.
facts.hook: A child wants to splash in the waves right away and waits until a grown-up comes down to the water with her.

facts.fact: When a family gets home from a trip, they unpack their bags and put things away.
facts.hook: Tired after the trip, a child finds sand in her shoes while unpacking and laughs about the beach.

facts.fact: Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day.
facts.hook: A child notices the new kitten's water bowl is empty and helps a grown-up fill it with fresh water.

facts.fact: A leash clipped to a dog's collar keeps the dog close to the person walking it.
facts.hook: The new puppy wants to chase a bird, and the child is glad the grown-up holding the leash keeps it close.

facts.fact: An indoor cat uses a litter box as its toilet.
facts.hook: A child wonders where the new cat goes to the bathroom and a grown-up shows her the litter box.

facts.fact: A veterinarian, or vet, is a doctor for animals.
facts.hook: A child worries the new puppy is going to a people doctor and is surprised to find a waiting room full of pets.

facts.fact: Chocolate can make dogs very sick, so dogs are never given chocolate.
facts.hook: A child wants to share his chocolate treat with the new dog, and a grown-up gives him a dog treat to offer instead.

facts.fact: A new pet may hide at first while it gets used to its new home.
facts.hook: A child is sad when the new cat hides under the bed, so she sits quietly nearby and waits for it to come out.

facts.fact: A small pet like a guinea pig is held gently with two hands while sitting down, so it cannot fall far.
facts.hook: A child wants to carry the guinea pig around the room, and a grown-up shows him how to sit on the floor to hold it.

facts.fact: A tag on a pet's collar tells people how to reach its family if the pet gets lost.
facts.hook: A child helps choose a name tag for the new puppy and asks why it needs the family's phone number on it.

facts.fact: It is a good habit to wash your hands after touching a pet or cleaning its cage.
facts.hook: A child runs to the snack table straight after petting the rabbit and turns back to wash her hands first.

facts.fact: At an animal shelter, pets wait for a family to adopt them and take them home.
facts.hook: At the shelter, a child walks past many dogs and cats, looking for the one that will come home with them.

facts.fact: When a pet is sleeping or eating, it is best to leave it alone.
facts.hook: A child wants to play with the new dog while it eats dinner and learns to wait until the bowl is empty.

facts.fact: When you count, you say one number word for each object and count each object only once.
facts.hook: A child counts the same apple twice and gets the wrong number, then counts again pointing at each apple once.

facts.fact: The last number you say when counting tells how many there are altogether.
facts.hook: Asked how many cookies are on the plate, a child counts 'one, two, three, four' and then proudly says 'four!'

facts.fact: You can start counting a group from any object, and the total stays the same.
facts.hook: Two friends count the same toy cars starting from opposite ends and are surprised to get the same number.

facts.fact: Spreading objects out or pushing them close together does not change how many there are.
facts.hook: A child thinks the spread-out buttons are more than the bunched-up ones until he counts both rows.

facts.fact: Lining two groups up side by side, one across from one, shows which has more: the group with some left over.
facts.hook: Two children argue over who has more blocks, so they line them up in pairs and see whose row is longer.

facts.fact: Two groups have the same number when each object in one group can be matched with one object in the other.
facts.hook: A child puts one cup in front of each chair at the table and finds there is exactly one for everyone.

facts.fact: Big objects and small objects count the same: three big balls and three tiny beads are both three.
facts.hook: A child thinks the three big balls are more than the three beads, then counts both and finds they match.

facts.fact: Adding one more object to a group makes the number go up to the next counting number.
facts.hook: A child has four stickers, gets one more from Grandma, and counts to find she now has five.

facts.fact: Taking one object away from a group makes the number one smaller.
facts.hook: A child counts five strawberries, eats one, and counts again to see how many are left.

facts.fact: Zero means none, so an empty plate has zero cookies on it.
facts.hook: A child counts the cookies as they are eaten until the plate is empty and learns the word for none.

facts.fact: 'Fewer' is the opposite of 'more': when one group has more, the other group has fewer.
facts.hook: At the corner store, a child picks the bag with fewer candies by mistake and learns the word for it.

facts.fact: Holding up one finger for each thing you count helps you keep track of the number.
facts.hook: A child loses count of the birds on the fence, then tries again putting up a finger for each bird.

facts.fact: Asking 'Can I have a turn when you're done?' lets a friend know you are waiting.
facts.hook: A child reaches for the swing, stops, and asks for the next turn instead.

facts.fact: Grabbing a toy out of someone's hands can make them feel sad or angry.
facts.hook: A child grabs a friend's truck, sees the friend start to cry, and gives it back to ask properly.

facts.fact: Taking turns means one person plays for a while, and then the other person gets to play.
facts.hook: Two children both want the one toy drum, so they agree to take turns banging it.

facts.fact: A sand timer can show when a turn is over: when the sand runs out, the turn ends.
facts.hook: Arguing over the scooter, two children use a sand timer and watch the sand to know whose turn is next.

facts.fact: While you wait for a turn, you can play with something else.
facts.hook: Waiting for the slide feels too long, so a child builds a sandcastle until it is her turn.

facts.fact: Sharing means letting someone else use or play with something too.
facts.hook: A child has the whole box of crayons and notices a friend with none, so she pushes the box to the middle.

facts.fact: Playing with one toy together, like building one tower side by side, is another way to share.
facts.hook: Two children both want the blocks and decide to build one big tower together.

facts.fact: If two children want the same toy, a grown-up can help them take turns.
facts.hook: Two children tug on the same doll at a party, then ask a grown-up for help deciding who goes first.

facts.fact: Waiting can feel hard, and taking slow, deep breaths can help you stay calm while you wait.
facts.hook: A child feels like grabbing the ball, so he takes three slow breaths while his friend finishes his turn.

facts.fact: When your turn is over, you hand the toy gently to the next person.
facts.hook: When the timer runs out, a child almost tosses the toy, then hands it over gently instead.

facts.fact: When a friend shares with you, saying 'thank you' shows you noticed their kindness.
facts.hook: A friend lets a child have the red bucket, and the child remembers to say thank you before running off.

facts.fact: A very special toy can be put away before friends come over, so you don't have to share it.
facts.hook: Before a playdate, a child worries about his favorite bear and puts it on a high shelf, then shares his other toys.

facts.fact: A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read.
facts.hook: A child finds a book she loves at the library and is thrilled to learn her new card means she can take it home.

facts.fact: Borrowed books have to be brought back to the library by a certain day, called the due date.
facts.hook: A child wants to keep a borrowed book forever and learns it has to go back so others can read it.

facts.fact: A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card.
facts.hook: A child wants a card of his own and goes to the desk with a grown-up to sign up for it.

facts.fact: Library books are shared with many other people, so we take care not to tear or write in them.
facts.hook: A child almost draws in a library book, then decides to draw on her own paper instead.

facts.fact: Many libraries ask people to use quiet voices so others can read.
facts.hook: A child shouts with excitement about a dinosaur book and then whispers when he sees people reading.

facts.fact: A book return slot is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library.
facts.hook: A child is worried to let go of her book into the return slot, then waves it goodbye.

facts.fact: Many libraries have a children's area with books just for young kids.
facts.hook: A child looks at tall shelves of grown-up books and is happy to find the colorful children's corner.

facts.fact: At storytime, a librarian reads books aloud to a group of children.
facts.hook: A child is shy about joining storytime, then sits down when the librarian opens a funny book.

facts.fact: Library books have a label on the spine that shows where the book belongs on the shelf.
facts.hook: A child puts a book back in the wrong place, and the librarian shows him how the spine label helps.

facts.fact: A library card can be used again and again to borrow new books.
facts.hook: After returning her first book, a child is excited to find she can borrow a new one with the same card.

facts.fact: A librarian is a person who works at the library and helps people find books.
facts.hook: A child can't find any books about trucks, so she asks the librarian for help.

facts.fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
facts.hook: A child counts 'one, two, four' and his big sister helps him find the missing number.

facts.fact: Counting backward from ten down to one is called a countdown.
facts.hook: Playing rocket ship, a child counts down from ten and jumps up on 'blast off!'

facts.fact: In hide-and-seek, the seeker counts while the others hide.
facts.hook: A child counts too fast in hide-and-seek, and her friends ask her to count slowly so they can hide.

facts.fact: In the song 'Five Little Monkeys Jumping on the Bed', one monkey falls off each time, so the number gets one smaller.
facts.hook: A child sings the song with toy monkeys and takes one away each verse to see how many are left.

facts.fact: The rhyme 'One, Two, Buckle My Shoe' puts the counting words into a rhyme.
facts.hook: A child can't remember what comes after two, so she sings the rhyme to help her.

facts.fact: A number word always means the same amount: 'three' always means three things.
facts.hook: A child is told he can have three grapes and wonders if big grapes count differently.

facts.fact: There are seven days in a week.
facts.hook: A child wants to know how long until Saturday and counts the days of the week on her fingers.

facts.fact: A pair means two, like a pair of socks.
facts.hook: A child finds one sock and learns he needs to find its partner to make a pair.

facts.fact: The word 'five' and the numeral 5 mean the same number.
facts.hook: A child sees the numeral 5 on a door and realizes it is the same five she counts on her fingers.

facts.fact: Ten is written with two digits, a 1 and then a 0.
facts.hook: A child tries to write ten and wonders why it needs two numbers when the others need only one.

facts.fact: A child's age is said with a number word, like 'I am four.'
facts.hook: A child holds up fingers when asked her age, then says the number word out loud.

facts.fact: People say 'please' when they ask for something.
facts.hook: A child says 'Give me juice!' at the dinner table, then tries again with 'please.'

facts.fact: People say 'thank you' after someone gives them something or helps them.
facts.hook: A child runs off with the ball a friend passed him, then turns back to say thank you.

facts.fact: Saying 'sorry' shows you feel bad when you hurt someone or make a mistake.
facts.hook: A child knocks over a friend's sandcastle by accident and says sorry before helping to rebuild it.

facts.fact: Saying 'excuse me' is a polite way to get past someone who is in your way.
facts.hook: In a busy store aisle, a child tries to squeeze past a shopper and remembers to say excuse me.

facts.fact: When someone says 'thank you', people often answer 'you're welcome.'
facts.hook: A friend thanks a child for sharing her snack, and she isn't sure what to say back.

facts.fact: Saying 'Can you help me, please?' is a way to ask for help when something is too hard.
facts.hook: A child gets frustrated with a stuck jar lid at the table and asks a grown-up for help with the right words.

facts.fact: It is polite to wait until someone finishes talking before you start to speak.
facts.hook: A child keeps interrupting a grown-up at dinner, then learns to wait for a pause to share her news.

facts.fact: Saying 'hello' when you meet someone is a friendly way to greet them.
facts.hook: A child hides behind a grown-up when a neighbor waves at the park, then peeks out and says hello.

facts.fact: Saying 'no, thank you' is a polite way to say you don't want something.
facts.hook: A child is offered a food she doesn't like and shouts 'yuck!', then tries again with 'no, thank you.'

facts.fact: Starting a question with 'May I' is a polite way to ask permission.
facts.hook: A child wants to hold a friend's kite and asks 'May I have a turn?' instead of just taking it.

facts.fact: Other languages have their own words for thank you, like 'gracias' in Spanish.
facts.hook: A new friend at the park says 'gracias,' and a child learns to say it back.

facts.fact: A circle is round and has no corners.
facts.hook: A child looks for a corner on a paper circle to start cutting and discovers there isn't one.

facts.fact: A square has four sides that are all the same length.
facts.hook: A child isn't sure if a cracker is a square, so he measures its sides with a piece of string.

facts.fact: A triangle has three sides and three corners.
facts.hook: A child counts the corners of a sandwich cut into triangles before taking a bite.

facts.fact: A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, like the shape of a door.
facts.hook: Hunting for rectangles in the classroom, a child spots the door and counts its corners.

facts.fact: Wheels are round like circles, which lets them roll.
facts.hook: A child makes a toy car with square cardboard wheels, finds it won't roll, and cuts circles instead.

facts.fact: Cutting a square from one corner to the opposite corner makes two triangles.
facts.hook: A child wants two triangles for a paper sailboat but has only a square, so a grown-up shows where to cut.

facts.fact: Folding a square piece of paper in half, edge to edge, makes a rectangle.
facts.hook: A child folds a square napkin in half and is surprised by the new shape.

facts.fact: A square turned so a corner points up is still a square.
facts.hook: A child says the tilted block is a new shape, then turns it back and sees it is the same square.

facts.fact: A cube, like a toy block, has six flat faces, and each one is a square.
facts.hook: A child counts the faces of a block by putting a sticker on each one.

facts.fact: Tracing around the bottom of a round cup draws a circle.
facts.hook: A child's hand-drawn circles come out wobbly, so she traces around a cup instead.

facts.fact: A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles, because size does not change a shape.
facts.hook: A child says a small button can't be a circle like the big clock, then compares the two.

facts.fact: Cooks wash their hands with soap and water before they touch food.
facts.hook: A child runs in from the backyard wanting to stir the batter, and Grandma points to the sink first.

facts.fact: A grown-up is in charge of the hot stove and oven when children help cook.
facts.hook: A child wants to check the cookies alone, then waits for Dad to open the oven.

facts.fact: Measuring cups and spoons help cooks put in the right amount of each thing.
facts.hook: A child pours sugar straight from the bag, then learns to fill the measuring cup instead.

facts.fact: A recipe tells a cook what to use and what to do, one step at a time.
facts.hook: The pancakes come out flat because a step was skipped, so the family reads the recipe again.

facts.fact: Cooks crack an egg's shell open to get the egg out.
facts.hook: A bit of shell falls into the bowl, and the child fishes it out with a spoon.

facts.fact: Butter from the fridge is hard, and butter left out on the counter gets softer.
facts.hook: A child can't spread cold butter on the bread, so they set it out and wait.

facts.fact: Flour is a dry powder that makes a little cloud when it is poured fast.
facts.hook: A child dumps the flour in quickly and everyone gets a dusty nose, so next time they pour slowly.

facts.fact: Cooks knead bread dough by pushing and folding it with their hands.
facts.hook: A child thinks the sticky dough is ruined until Mom shows how to push and fold it.

facts.fact: Cake batter is runny when it goes into the oven and comes out as a cake you can slice.
facts.hook: A child worries the runny batter will never be a birthday cake, then sees the grown-up take out a real cake.

facts.fact: Cooks rinse dirt off vegetables like carrots and potatoes before cooking them.
facts.hook: Carrots from the farmers' market still have dirt on them, and the child scrubs them in the sink.

facts.fact: A kitchen timer beeps or rings to tell the cook it is time to check the food.
facts.hook: The family gets busy playing a game, and the timer's beep reminds them about the muffins.

facts.fact: When a grown-up cuts an onion, it can make their eyes sting and water.
facts.hook: A child thinks Dad is sad because he is crying, then learns it is only the onion.

facts.fact: Bike riders wear a helmet to keep their head safe if they fall.
facts.hook: A child is in a hurry to ride and forgets the helmet, then runs back for it.

facts.fact: A bike without training wheels has just two wheels, one in front and one behind.
facts.hook: A child counts the wheels after the training wheels come off and finds only two.

facts.fact: Training wheels are two small extra wheels at the back that keep a bike from tipping over.
facts.hook: A child watches a grown-up take the training wheels off and wonders how the bike will stay up.

facts.fact: Pushing the pedals around makes a bike roll forward.
facts.hook: A child sits on the bike waiting for it to move, then remembers to push the pedals.

facts.fact: Turning the handlebars makes the bike turn left or right.
facts.hook: A child heads toward the grass and turns the handlebars just in time to stay on the path.

facts.fact: Bikes have brakes that the rider uses to slow down and stop.
facts.hook: A child rolls too far down the driveway, then practices using the brakes to stop at a chalk line.

facts.fact: A bike is easier to balance when it is moving than when it is standing still.
facts.hook: A child keeps tipping while stopped, then finds it steadier once the wheels are rolling.

facts.fact: A grown-up can hold the back of the seat and walk or run beside a child who is learning.
facts.hook: A child is scared to try until Mom promises to hold the seat and run alongside.

facts.fact: When a bike stops, the rider puts a foot down on the ground to stay up.
facts.hook: A child stops, wobbles and tips, then learns to put a foot down.

facts.fact: New riders practice in safe places away from cars, like a path, a driveway or an empty parking lot.
facts.hook: A child wants to ride on the street, and the family goes to the empty parking lot instead.

facts.fact: A bike bell rings to let people nearby know a bike is coming.
facts.hook: A walker on the bike path doesn't hear the child coming, so the child rings the bell.

facts.fact: When bike tires get soft, a grown-up pumps more air into them.
facts.hook: The bike feels slow and bumpy, and Grandpa finds a soft tire and pumps it up.

facts.fact: A grandparent is a parent of your mom or your dad.
facts.hook: A child is surprised to learn that Grandma is Mom's mom.

facts.fact: A week has seven days.
facts.hook: A child marks each day of Grandpa's visit on the calendar and counts to seven.

facts.fact: Guests who come to stay pack their clothes and things in a suitcase or bag.
facts.hook: A child helps pull Grandma's suitcase in from the car and wonders what is inside.

facts.fact: Families get a bed or sleeping spot ready for a guest who stays the night.
facts.hook: A child picks out a soft pillow and a favorite blanket for Grandpa's bed.

facts.fact: At an airport, families wait in the arrivals area to meet people coming off a plane.
facts.hook: A child watches the arrivals doors and keeps thinking every person is Grandma.

facts.fact: At a train station, people wait on the platform and stand back from the edge until the train stops.
facts.hook: A child wants to lean out to see the train coming, then steps back behind the line with Dad.

facts.fact: A grandparent can tell stories about when a child's mom or dad was little.
facts.hook: A child can't imagine Dad as a little boy until Grandma tells about his first bike.

facts.fact: A child can greet a grandparent with a hug, a wave, or a hello.
facts.hook: A shy child isn't ready for a hug at the station and waves hello instead.

facts.fact: Hosts show a guest where things are, like the towels and the bathroom.
facts.hook: Grandpa can't find a towel after his bath, so the child shows him the cupboard.

facts.fact: A grandparent can show a child how to make a food their family has made for a long time.
facts.hook: In the kitchen, a child learns Grandma's way to make her special bread.

facts.fact: Grandparents and children can play card games or board games together, taking turns.
facts.hook: A child wants to go first every time, and Grandpa shows how taking turns works.

facts.fact: After a visit ends, families can stay in touch with phone calls, video calls or letters.
facts.hook: A child is sad when Grandma leaves, then draws her a picture to send in a letter.

facts.fact: A steady beat stays even and keeps going, like footsteps when you march.
facts.hook: A child claps faster and faster until they march around the room to feel the steady beat.

facts.fact: Clapping along to the beat means clapping at the same time as the beat of the music.
facts.hook: A child claps whenever they like, then listens and matches their claps to the song.

facts.fact: You can keep the beat by tapping your knees, stamping your feet or tapping a drum.
facts.hook: A child's hands get tired of clapping, so they stamp the beat with their feet instead.

facts.fact: Nursery rhymes are short rhyming songs or poems for young children.
facts.hook: A child asks Grandpa for a nursery rhyme and he teaches one he knew as a boy.

facts.fact: Rhyming words end with the same sound, like cat and hat.
facts.hook: A child forgets a word in the rhyme and guesses it by finding a word that rhymes.

facts.fact: Singing a song again and again helps you learn its words by heart.
facts.hook: A child can't remember the second line until they have sung the rhyme many times.

facts.fact: A song can be sung loudly or softly.
facts.hook: A child sings as loud as they can, then tries the lullaby softly for a sleeping baby.

facts.fact: A song can be played or sung fast or slow.
facts.hook: The class sings a rhyme very fast and gets tangled, then tries it slowly.

facts.fact: 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' and the ABC song use the same tune.
facts.hook: A child humming the ABC song notices it sounds just like 'Twinkle, Twinkle.'

facts.fact: Some songs have hand actions, like the spider climbing up in 'The Itsy Bitsy Spider.'
facts.hook: A child mixes up the actions and has the spider climb down, then fixes it.

facts.fact: A music teacher may count 'one, two, three, four' so everyone starts singing together.
facts.hook: A child starts singing too early and learns to wait for the count.

facts.fact: At a concert, people in the audience clap when the music is over to show they enjoyed it.
facts.hook: A child starts clapping in the middle of a quiet song, then waits for the end.

facts.fact: A beanbag lands with a soft flop instead of bouncing like a ball.
facts.hook: A child expects the beanbag to bounce into the hoop and sees it flop down instead.

facts.fact: Looking at the target while you throw helps you aim.
facts.hook: A child throws while looking at a friend and misses, then tries again looking at the hoop.

facts.fact: Standing closer to the hoop makes it easier to get the beanbag in.
facts.hook: A child keeps missing from far away and takes a few steps closer.

facts.fact: In an underhand throw, your arm swings from low down, forward and up.
facts.hook: A child throws overhand and the beanbag flies past, so the teacher shows an underhand toss.

facts.fact: Catching a big ball is easier with two hands than with one.
facts.hook: A child tries to catch the ball with one hand like a big kid, then uses both hands.

facts.fact: Watching the ball all the way to your hands helps you catch it.
facts.hook: A child shuts their eyes as the ball comes and misses, then keeps their eyes open.

facts.fact: Holding your arms out with your hands open gets you ready to catch.
facts.hook: A child's hands are in their pockets when the ball comes, so next time they hold them out.

facts.fact: Hugging the ball to your chest helps you hold on to it after you catch it.
facts.hook: The ball keeps bouncing out of a child's hands until they hug it in.

facts.fact: A gentle toss is easier to catch than a hard, fast throw.
facts.hook: A child throws the ball too hard to a little friend, then tries a gentle toss.

facts.fact: Taking turns means one person throws, and then the next person has a turn.
facts.hook: A child wants to throw all the beanbags and learns to pass them to the next child.

facts.fact: Practicing again and again makes throwing and catching get easier.
facts.hook: A child is upset after missing, keeps practicing in the backyard, and gets one in.

facts.fact: Plants in a garden or on a windowsill need sunlight to grow.
facts.hook: A child hides a plant in a dark closet as a surprise and it looks poorly, so they move it to the window.

facts.fact: When you water a plant in a pot, you pour the water onto the soil.
facts.hook: A child sprinkles water only on the leaves, then learns to pour it on the soil.

facts.fact: Rain gives water to plants that grow outside.
facts.hook: A child wants to water the backyard garden, but it rained, so the soil is already wet.

facts.fact: Pets need their people to give them food.
facts.hook: A child is busy playing and the cat sits by its empty bowl until the child remembers.

facts.fact: A pet dog or cat needs a bowl of clean water it can drink from.
facts.hook: A child sees the dog's water bowl is empty on a hot day and fills it.

facts.fact: A pet rabbit eats plants, like hay and leafy greens.
facts.hook: A child wants to share a cookie with the rabbit, then gives it hay instead.

facts.fact: Many birds build nests to hold their eggs and baby birds.
facts.hook: A child spots a nest in a tree and watches from far away with a grown-up.

facts.fact: An animal's home can be a nest, a burrow, a pond, or a hole in a tree.
facts.hook: On a forest walk, a child looks for animal homes and finds a hole in a tree.

facts.fact: Squirrels bury or hide nuts to eat later.
facts.hook: A child watches a squirrel dig in the backyard and wonders what it's hiding.

facts.fact: At a pet store, people buy food and homes like cages and tanks for their pets.
facts.hook: A family at the pet store remembers they need food, not just a new toy, for their hamster.

facts.fact: Things can be sorted into groups, like animals, toys and foods.
facts.hook: A child dumps out a basket of pictures and sorts them into piles.

facts.fact: Apples, bread and carrots are all foods.
facts.hook: A child puts the carrot with the toys, then moves it to the food group.

facts.fact: Dogs, cows and fish are all animals.
facts.hook: A child thinks a fish is not an animal because it has no legs, then learns it is.

facts.fact: Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys.
facts.hook: In the playroom, a child fills the toy box and names each toy that goes in.

facts.fact: A toy dog is a toy, not an animal, because it is not alive.
facts.hook: A child puts the stuffed dog in the animal pile, then thinks again.

facts.fact: One thing can belong to more than one group, like an apple is a food and also a fruit.
facts.hook: Two children argue whether the apple goes with the fruits or the foods, and learn both are right.

facts.fact: Birds are animals that have feathers.
facts.hook: A child finds a feather in the backyard and knows a bird must have lost it.

facts.fact: Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes.
facts.hook: A child sorting the laundry puts a sock with the toys, then laughs and moves it.

facts.fact: Things can also be sorted by color, size or shape.
facts.hook: A child sorts blocks by color, then a friend sorts the same blocks by size.

facts.fact: The odd one out is the thing that does not belong in a group.
facts.hook: A child spots a banana hidden among toy cars and calls it the odd one out.

facts.fact: A library puts its books on shelves in groups so people can find them.
facts.hook: A child wants a book about animals, and the librarian shows the shelf of animal books.

facts.fact: In a power cut, electric lights go off and do not come on when you flip the switch.
facts.hook: A child keeps flipping the light switch and nothing happens.

facts.fact: A flashlight with working batteries still shines when the power is out.
facts.hook: The family can't find the flashlight in the dark, and a child remembers the kitchen drawer.

facts.fact: If a family uses candles, only a grown-up lights them and looks after them.
facts.hook: A child wants to carry a candle to their room and gets a flashlight instead.

facts.fact: In a power cut, families keep the fridge door shut so the food inside stays cold longer.
facts.hook: A child wants to open the fridge to look for a snack and learns to keep it shut.

facts.fact: In the dark, your eyes slowly get used to it, and you can see more after a little while.
facts.hook: At first a child can't see anything, then slowly makes out the shape of the sofa.

facts.fact: Shining a flashlight on your hands can make shadow shapes on the wall.
facts.hook: A bored child makes a shadow bunny on the wall with a flashlight.

facts.fact: Books, puzzles and board games can be played without electricity.
facts.hook: A child is upset the TV won't work, then the family plays a board game by flashlight.

facts.fact: In the dark, walk slowly and hold a grown-up's hand so nobody trips.
facts.hook: A child runs to the kitchen in the dark and bumps into a chair, then holds Dad's hand.

facts.fact: Storms with strong wind can knock out the power.
facts.hook: The wind howls outside, the lights go out, and the family gathers in the living room.

facts.fact: In a power cut, the house gets quieter because machines like the fridge stop humming.
facts.hook: A child notices how quiet the house is and listens for sounds they never heard before.

facts.fact: A power cut can make all the houses on a street go dark at once.
facts.hook: A child looks out the window and sees the neighbors' houses are dark too.

facts.fact: After a power cut, clocks on the oven or microwave may blink and need to be set again.
facts.hook: When the lights come back, a child notices the oven clock blinking and helps Mom fix it.

facts.fact: A snow day is a day when school is closed because of snow.
facts.hook: A child wakes up ready for school and hears it is a snow day.

facts.fact: People wear hats, mittens, boots and warm coats to play in the snow.
facts.hook: A child runs out without mittens, gets cold fingers, and comes back for them.

facts.fact: Snow melts into water when it is brought inside where it is warm.
facts.hook: A child brings a snowball inside to keep and finds a puddle later.

facts.fact: Snow that is a little wet packs together well for making a snowman.
facts.hook: A child's snowman keeps falling apart in dry snow, then works when the snow gets stickier.

facts.fact: Feet leave footprints in fresh snow.
facts.hook: A child follows footprints in the snow and finds they lead to the neighbor's door.

facts.fact: Lying in the snow and sweeping your arms and legs makes a snow angel.
facts.hook: A child makes a snow angel but stands up in the middle and smudges it, then tries again.

facts.fact: At a sledding hill, children sled sitting up and facing forward with a grown-up watching.
facts.hook: A child wants to go down head first, and Dad shows how to sit up and hold on.

facts.fact: Grown-ups shovel snow off paths so people can walk without slipping.
facts.hook: A child helps with a small shovel to clear the path for the mail carrier.

facts.fact: Icy ground is slippery, so people walk slowly and carefully on it.
facts.hook: A child runs on the icy sidewalk and slips, then takes small, slow steps.

facts.fact: A snowplow pushes snow off the road.
facts.hook: A child watches from the window as a big snowplow scrapes down the street.

facts.fact: Wet mittens and boots are left out to dry after playing in the snow.
facts.hook: A child wants to go back out but their mittens are soaked, so they hang them to dry first.
